CALL FOR INCREASED EXPORTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. As the $1 billion loss in Canada's grain export program so far this year is seen by many producers as a deliberate attempt by the government to hold down inflation and economic activity in the prairies, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That the government bring in new and innovative measures to increase exports before grain producers are killed off economically and told by the responsible minister that it is all for their own good.

subsubtopic: ACTIVITIES OF SO-CALLED RELIGIOUS CULTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent necessity. In light of the recent tragic events in a so-called religious community in Jonestown, Guyana; in light of the fact that the Scientology cult has operated in a clandestine fashion, including the theft of government documents within the federal government of the United States; in light of the fact that the Children of God cult has influenced young Canadian women in Europe to serve as "hookers for Jesus" to raise funds for the cult; and, finally, in light of the fact that some of these cults have destroyed the family unit, creating untold heartbreak for the parents, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That the government, bearing in mind the rights of individuals to religious freedom, give consideration to the necessity of inquiring into the activities of these so-called religious cults.

REQUEST GOVERNMENT RECONSIDER DECISION RESPECTING YUGOSLAVIAN REFUGEES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with an urgent question of pressing necessity.
Considering that the Government of Canada wishes to offer political asylum to 600 refugees aboard the Hai Hong who will be entirely dependent on Canadians; considering that the government denies political asylum to three Yugoslavian refugees who are prepared to invest $675,000 in a lumber company in the Val-d'Or area; and considering that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) has shown inconsistency by rejecting individuals who are anxious to serve the country while he accepts refugees who will be on social welfare, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the House condemn the decision of the Minister of Employment and Immigration about the three Yugoslavian refugees and immediately enjoin the minister to review his decision and encourage immigrants who can really help our country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to ask the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion relating to a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the Winnipeg office of the Canadian Forestry Service may be closed because of the government's restraint program, since Dutch elm disease now is well established in Manitoba, particularly along the banks of the Red River, and since the Canadian Forestry Service was the only agency acting against the spread of Dutch elm disease, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway):
That this House instructs the Department of the Environment to establish immediately an alternative and active program to combat Dutch elm disease in order to prevent complete desecration of the Red River treeline.

subsubtopic: EFFICIENCY OF POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: An hon. member asks, why? I think the answer to that question is clear. We believe the extent of postal subsidies is a key element in cultural strategy of the federal government. It was, therefore, felt appropriate-and I think it is appropriate-that that responsibility of recommendation in the development of policy ideas should rest with the Secretary of State, whose general responsibility that is.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. As the minister knows, Secretary of State Cyrus Vance will be meeting with the Prime Minister and a number of ministers of the Crown, presumably tomorrow, to discuss important matters.
Since the U.S. ambassador to Canada said yesterday in Windsor presumably with a straight face, that Canada was getting more than its share of jobs under the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement, a statement which flies in the face of an Ontario government study which shows that for years we have had fewer jobs than would warrant in our share of the market, could the minister tell the House whether he or the Prime Minister will be putting before Mr. Vance specific proposals to ensure that we at long last, will get a fair deal from the auto pact?
Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and
Commerce): Mr. Speaker, I am certain that if Mr. Vance wants to discuss the auto pact with the Prime Minister or myself we are prepared to discuss it. We do not accept the figures that the Ontario government gave with regard to employment. I can say to the House that employment in the automobile industry is up substantially this year over what it was last year. Our deficit with the United States in auto parts and automobiles is down considerably from what it was last year.

INCREASE IN AIRPORT TAX-EFFECT ON TOURIST INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. In light of the announcement last week of the increase in air transportation tax from $8 to $15 in the case of domestic flights, and $8 to $12 in the case of international flights, and the fact that the domestic increase will take place in April while the international increase will take effect in July, can the minister explain the apparent discrimination against the domestic air traveller? Does he agree with this particular concept? Can he outline, in particular, his position with regard to this increase relative to the increase in our tourist trade deficit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport and Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: INCREASE IN AIRPORT TAX-EFFECT ON TOURIST INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I certainly would not agree that there is any discrimination against travellers in Canada as compared to travellers abroad. The apparent discrimination in this airport tax is explained by the fact that there is already a very heavy discrimination, if you like, against the traveller abroad, in the sense that the fees now charged against that kind of travel are significantly higher than the domestic fees, landing fees and the like. There was not room, in our view, within the cost to us of international air travel, to increase those fees more than the $12 in the initial stages, as indicated. In other words, the lower international transportation tax really reflects the fact that the domestic user charges are much lower than the international user charges.

subtopic: INCREASE IN AIRPORT TAX-EFFECT ON TOURIST INDUSTRY
speechtext: Is the minister concerned about the apparent discrimination which will affect regional and third-level carriers and passengers using those carriers, inasmuch as the manner in which the tax is to be applied will be disproportionately more severe on those using third-level and regional air carriers, or is this part of an over-all strategy to rationalize the regional air carrier industry? Could the minister tell us whether he still intends to go ahead with this planned sixfold increase in airport user fees and other user fees associated with airports?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: INCREASE IN AIRPORT TAX-EFFECT ON TOURIST INDUSTRY
speechtext: It is very much our policy to encourage the development of the regional and third-level carriers. It might not be possible to contain special provisions for these carriers in an air transportation tax, but I can assure the hon. member that on the question of increases in any user charges we shall be looking very seriously at the question whether or not we can give special consideration to the third-level carriers and to the regionals in order to lighten the load upon them.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. On February 2 of this year the minister reported to the House that there was general agreement, at a meeting of tourism ministers on January 31, that present costs impede

our country when it comes to the successful balancing of tourist accounts. In June, Statistics Canada reported that travel costs for Canadians rose 71.5 per cent between 1971 and 1977, much faster than the 50 per cent gain shown in the United States. This year, the number of American tourists coming to Canada is down by 1 per cent so far.
In view of these facts, why did the minister permit the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Transport to impose an almost doubling of the air transportation tax? Will the minister now have this reversed and, therefore, have the government practice what it preaches in trying to control costs in connection with tourism?
Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and
Commerce): As I said the other day in answer to the same question, I, as a tourist, would like to feel I am paying my way in whatever host country I decide to visit. Certainly, as a Canadian taxpayer who may decide to stay at home, I believe tourists who come to this country should pay whatever costs are incurred by our government and our taxpayers. It is that simple, really. If the costs are justified, the tourist should pay them.
That's it. They are not.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member says, "That's it. They are not." Certainly, I believe air transportation is becoming very reasonable to Canadians. We have brought in a number of measures. Something like 314 more ABC flights within Canada were used last summer to convince Canadians to travel far cheaper in their own country.

The minister's replies are balderdash, which means "nonsense", as the Deputy Prime Minister may know. On September 1, at a Toronto press conference, the minister said:
Canadians traditionally have the idea that tourists are somebody we can rip off when they are going through-charge them all we can and then let them go.
The minister went on to say we have a lot to learn about hospitality when treating strangers. How does he square that criticism of the Canadian tourist industry and the hotels and motels of this country with the government's action in ripping off tourists, both Canadian and foreign, in this manner? How does the minister justify that rip-off? Or is there some difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not accept the fact that there is a rip-off at all. I believe the costs are justified and that the tourists should pay them. I could point out that tourism from Japan is up 28 per cent and that tourism from Europe this year is up 20 per cent, so the tourism deficit is not growing at all.

MR. FRIESEN-BROADCASTING OF CBC LICENCE RENEWAL APPLICATION PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Last October 23 the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) raised a question of privilege in the House, and since I was not present at that time you deferred the matter until you had a chance to have me reply to him. Since both the hon. member and I are in the House this afternoon, I thought I might reply to him.
His question of privilege essentially was that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation had not covered his remarks to the CRTC at the CRTC hearing. I have the information which the CBC has presented to me on the matter, which is relatively brief, and I would be happy to explain to the House its position at the present time in relation to the hon. member's question of privilege.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation rents four satellite channels for transmission of its television programming. One of these, Channel D, is used for closed circuit purposes, for gathering and distributing news items, for the exchange of regional programs and inserts, and for multi-point live productions. The CBC decided to make coverage of the CRTC hearings on its network licence renewal applications widely available, and made arrangements with a number of cable companies to carry the coverage across the country. Although

November 21, 1978
Privilege-Mr. Friesen
it was intended that as much of the hearings as possible should be covered, there were technical limitations because of the necessity of continuing to distribute the items normally carried on Channel D. For this purpose, 1 p.m. to shortly after 2 p.m. each day was set aside for such distribution.
The CRTC was aware of this limitation and mentioned the 1 p.m. satellite cut-off time several times during the hearing. Indeed, the chairman, Dr. Camu, reminded the hearing of it immediately before the hon. member began his intervention at approximately 12.57 p.m. on October 6. The only area of the country not affected by the cut-off was Ottawa, where coverage was by direct cable service.
The hon. member's presentation lasted until about 1.16 p.m., and while the CBC regrets that his intervention was not received by those cable services outside Ottawa which had agreed to take the CRTC coverage, it would emphasize that, in accordance with the exigencies of broadcasting the prearranged schedule, it was necessary to provide its network stations with the other programming items they were then set up to receive.

I do not want to carry on the argument interminably, sir, but I have looked at this matter for some time now and if, as the minister says, I was admitted to the table at about three minutes to one and it was customary for the CRTC to call the lunch break at one o'clock-and far be it for them to postpone the lunch hour, either for them or for the intervenors-then it seems to me a blatant piece of disorganization to have, as the chairman said, the only member of parliament to appear before the committee appear at three minutes to one, just before it was time to break. Either that was a very sloppy piece of organization or it was a very deliberate attempt, but I cannot imagine that the chairman of the CRTC is the kind of person who would deliberately ask the only member of parliament to come to appear at three minutes before cut-off time to make his presentation. Since it did happen, Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether he did receive any kind of instructions.
I would add to that, Mr. Speaker, that I did check with people in the industry in the intervening days and I have found that it was not, as the minister said, at three minutes to one but considerably before that. While it may be that I could not have made my full presentation at that time, I could have made a considerable part of it. I still contend, Mr. Speaker, that there seems to be a deliberate decision made somewhere to make certain that my entire presentation would not be carried across Canada under the previous arrangements that were made available to all the other members who appeared.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for granting me time to raise this question of privilege today to refute incorrect statements made by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) in his November 10 question of privilege at page 1014 of Hansard in my absence, which related to the tabling date of the report of the Auditor General. As you know, I had intended to let this matter stand until later, but a third dimension has been brought to my attention and I feel I must set the record straight now.
The remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West not only aggrieved me but reflect on the performance and integrity of a member of the press gallery, if, in fact, they are not an attempt to muzzle the press.
Sir, in this democratic institution, honesty should not be ridiculed, for political expediency, or, indeed, for any reason. Often in this House press reporters are criticized for misinterpreting or misquoting members of parliament. My question of privilege today is in defence of a Canadian Press reporter who wrote a factual article, referred to by the hon. member for Ottawa West as "distortion of the facts". The statement attributed to me in the Canada Press story, and I quote: "I don't think we should be tinkering around with the report or with the date after it has already been announced" is exactly what I said in the public accounts committee.
The words included in that press account and quoted by the hon. member for Ottawa West in his question of privilege as, "It is clear the government does not want any criticism of its finances to come to light during the budget debate" were said by me outside committee and I stand behind them.
I do not condone placing blame on anyone else for anything I have said, and I certainly will not remain silent when the work of a member of the press gallery is unjustly placed in doubt, even if that writing happens to be inconvenient for the government or for any member of parliament.
My colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) said in the House on November 10, and I quote: "I would point out to Your Honour that the steering committee meetings are generally looked on as confidential matter." I

November 21, 1978
Point of Order-Mr. Abbott
agree with him. Under ordinary circumstances I would strictly adhere to that practice but, because the hon. member for Ottawa West made an incorrect statement in this House with reference to a steering committee meeting, I am compelled to refer to what actually transpired there.
This is the false statement of the hon. member for Ottawa West, in reference to the tabling of the Auditor General's report:
It was then unanimously agreed at the steering committee, at which the hon. member for Red Deer was present, that a more appropriate day might be Thursday, November 23.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a distortion of fact.
At the steering committee meeting I asked that the word "unanimous" not be used because I was not in agreement with postponing the tabling date of the report of the Auditor General to November 23.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Ottawa West should admit he misrepresented the facts as I have outlined, and should apologize to the member of the press gallery whose report did not "distort the facts." I might add that I abhor this type of attack in the House of Commons on anyone who does not have the opportunity to defend his or her position, which only adversely affects parliament and its members.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is of course a privilege to participate in the budget speech debate, although in this one it is difficult to do so with pleasure. That is because it is rather unusual to have a government bring in a

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
budget in which it congratulates itself on making things worse next year than they are this year.
Job creation, which was 362,000 this year, and not enough at that, will be 250,000 next year. The government also seemed proud of its deficit and intends to increase next year's deficit to a considerably higher level than this year's. It is rather reminiscent of the horse racing addict who made his way to the track saying, "I hope I do not lose too much today because I sure need the money!"
If I may be permitted to say a kind word about the unfortunate Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), I would point out that he seemed to be more comfortable when he was the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) then began to move around his chessmen in order to make room for his acquisition from Crowfoot. I hope the word "acquisition" is parliamentary. I would not want to get into the semantic argument as to whether the hon. member for Crowfoot was bought, purchased, acquired, given away, was obtained on waivers, or played out his option. The fact is the Prime Minister was acting as godfather of the family opposite and made him an offer he could not refuse.
In any case, the shifting around did a disservice to both those portfolios. We now have cabinet ministers in both Industry, Trade and Commerce and Finance who seem to be in difficulty. The self-confessed street fighter is beginning to look a little punchy, I am afraid.
A few days ago Mr. Speaker suggested to the splinter party on our left that if they wished to discuss defence they should not do so courtesy of Standing Order 26, but should take advantage of the opportunity of the budget debate. I welcome the Speaker's interest in defence. I hope we will hear from the party on the left in this debate. As well, I hope that at long last we will hear a few words from the minister about defence, defence being rather consistently underplayed in this House. There has been no mention whatsoever of defence in the last three throne speeches. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) does not seem to care to address this House very often on this subject. The last policy statement on defence by the government was in 1971 with the issuance of the so-called white paper.
Neither the country nor parliament at the present time has any idea of exactly what the government plans to do in the immediate and long-term future. I realize this particular lot of Liberals will mercifully be removed from guidance of national affairs before the medium future arrives. Even so, one would hope they would have done some planning during their too long regime.
This lack of planning is important, because the minister spends a significant amount of time addressing audiences outside of parliament, speaking about fantastic re-equipment programs which he and his predecessor have announced, as well as spurious versions of the amounts of money that this government is actually providing to National Defence, to buy equipment. The fact is that because of the deliberate downgrading of defence by the Prime Minister ever since he took over as leader of the Liberal party in 1968, we not only have a

crisis of obsolescence in nearly every field of the Armed Forces' equipment, but also an acute shortage of manpower, plus a vacuum in policy.
The fault for this situation lies entirely with successive Liberal governments, and the Ministers of National Defence who let both the equipment and the manpower of the forces run down so far that the over-all effectiveness of the forces is now at a disturbingly low level.
It is worth remembering that in 1963 the Armed Forces had
123,000	men. By 1968, when the present Prime Minister took power, there were 101,000, and today there are only 79,000, despite the promise made by the minister about a year ago that he was increasing the armed forces by 4,500. I suppose a lot of people in this country believed him. However, the increase so far has been in the order of 400.
In terms of equipment, the worst damage caused by the decade of neglect under the Liberals is still to come. Major weapons systems, like ships, fighters and tanks, have a useful life of 20 to 25 years, and they are extremely expensive. For this reason any responsible government ensures that it has a proper investment cycle whereby it replaces each year a portion of its heavy capital equipment. In this respect National Defence should not be any different from a large business organization. However, for eight years under the present Prime Minister, from 1968 to 1976, Canada did not place a single contract for a major weapon system, thereby distorting the investment cycle for capital requirements in the future.
Canadian taxpayers and the Armed Forces are going to have to pay for this long period of neglect, the Canadian taxpayers because they must foot the bill for buying 20 years of equipment over the next ten or 12 years, and the Canadian Armed Forces because they must suffer the effects of operating old and obsolete equipment. For the forces, though, the worst is still to come in some respects since there is no evidence the present minister intends to take action, as opposed to making endless promises, to ensure that enough new equipment will be delivered in time to maintain the effectiveness of the forces at even minimal levels.
Let us take a look at all three services, starting with the navy. At the present time we have a navy of 23 surface ships. If we exclude ships over 25 years old, by the time the six new frigates arrive in service we shall have only ten ships in our surface fleet, including the frigates-four left over from the present fleet and six new ships, for a ten-ship navy! How can Canada possibly carry out its commitments in ten years' time with only half the number of ships it has today? The question has particular relevance because the expansion of Canadian sovereignty into the 200-mile economic zone would certainly mean more, not fewer, tasks for the navy.
The Air Force is confronted by a more acute crisis involving timing, since decisions with regard to the acquisition of a new fighter which should have been taken before now have still not been taken by the government. At present the Air Force operates three different types of fighter aircraft. When first
November 21, 1978

bought by Canada they numbered over 400 planes in total. The most modern of our existing planes, the CF-5, is also the least capable, reflecting the fact that it was one of our poorest defence equipment choices since the war. Evidence of how little the Air Force thinks of this plane is shown by its wish to relegate it to an advanced trainer role as soon as the government provides the new fighter plane. The choice of the CF-5 in the sixties has, of course, made the present situation much worse because we are having to replace three types of fighter at once instead of just the much older CF-101 Voodoos and CF-104 Starfighters.
Let us turn to consider the current problem, the purchase of the new fighter aircraft. About a year ago the Minister of National Defence announced that tenders were being called to provide Canada with between 130 and 150 planes, and that six companies were being invited to participate. The date by which bids were to be entered-the government stressed it was to be the final date-was February 1, 1978. Five of the six companies put in their bids at that time; partly due to a technicality, the French company, Dussault, was not able to comply with the requirements and withdrew.
The project office proceeded to work on the mass of detail which had been given it in the way of bids, and under the policy direction of the cabinet selected a short list in the course of the following three and a half months. Flowever, during this period, partly due to the lack of credibility the government suffers in international circles-people were not certain the government meant what it said it meant-some of the aircraft companies sweetened their offers. Operating within the constraints placed upon it, the project office came up with a short list in June. The government, though, for some strange reason known only to its own paranoic circle, refused to admit, deny, or explain the presence of the short list.
I put a question to the Prime Minister on this subject at the time-it can be found on page 6716 of Hansard for June 26 last and might bear repeating at this point:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of National Defence I will direct my question to the Prime Minister. Can the right hon. gentleman confirm that the new fighter project management office has recommended that a short list of three planes be considered for the impending fighter contract, the F-16, the F-18A and the F-18L?
To which the Prime Minister replied:
I am not sure what the hon. member is quoting from and it is certainly not government policy.
The exchange continued:

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was not quoting from anything at that point except my own question, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps the Prime Minister has noted the following quotation from a Canadian Press release-"One of the options the cabinet is considering is the so-called short list, dropping some of the competing firms", Danson said.
Could the Prime Minister tell the House whether the choice is being dictated entirely by the fact that these three planes are the cheapest of those under consideration and that since only a fixed sum of money is available, S2.3 billion in 1977 dollars, other important factors such as air superiority qualities, range and target acquisition capability all have to be sacrificed in favour of financial considerations?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The question is truly hypothetical. However, I can tell the hon. member that we want to try to get the best plane for the least money.
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
Now, Mr. Speaker, here we are, five months later, once again discussing the short list. And once again it appears that the same three planes are under consideration.
What has caused this five months' delay? The Prime Minister told a press conference the other day that he had been requested by Mr. Schmidt of Germany to allow the company concerned a further opportunity to sweeten its offer in connection with the Panavia Tornado. I have nothing in particular against the extension which was granted on that occasion, though it did indicate a lack of managerial competence on the part of the government to the extent that it was not able, apparently, to convince prospective plane manufacturers that it was serious when it talked about the February 1 bids being final. Also, it indicated a lack of confidence in the government's own ability during the contract negotiation stage. As hon. members know, the companies were right and the government was wrong.
Be that as it may, August 1 was set as the date for the second and final bid. All plane manufacturing companies complied, although some of their second bids were almost identical to their first. But what has been the cause of the delay since August 1 ? We saw the unedifying spectable of the Minister of National Defence stating on September 6 that he would be presenting the short list to the cabinet committee on September 14 and to the full cabinet the following week, only to find that two months later he still has not done so. This raises several questions in the minds of parliamentarians, in the minds of the general public and, indeed, in the minds of those who manage the plane companies.
What is the purpose of this delay heaped on top of delay? There is one scenario, if I may use a phrase favoured by the Department of National Defence, which would provide all the answers to these repeated postponements. It is that the government intends to announce the new fighter aircraft at a time which would best serve the purposes of the Liberal party, that is, at a time close to a federal election. They will then announce the final selection, indicating to the forces that they are serious about this plane purchase, and, as they did so misleadingly in the case of the long-range patrol aircraft, they will indicate to all sectors of the country that all concerned are going to reap the benefits of increased employment resulting from the offset work. Speaking parenthetically on this aspect I might point out that the offset benefits accruing to British Columbia from the long-range patrol aircraft are now at the giddy height of one half of one per cent, up from one third of one per cent.
While the government still refuses formally to commit itself to a short list, the leaks coming out from cabinet meetings and from the minister's office indicate that the people influencing the choice of plane are a very odd lot indeed. It must be a little difficult for those members of the armed forces directly concerned with this plane to realize that the timing of the selection is being stage managed by Keith Davey, the rain maker who tells the Liberal party when to hold elections and what to do for months before the election, and that the final selection would depend largely on the Minister of Industry,

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan).
If I might, I would like to suggest to the Minister of National Defence that partisan advantages should be dropped at this time. The selection of this plane and the provision of this plane are a very, very important matter for the Armed Forces and for Canada. The most important factor that should be considered is the military requirement, not whether it will gain votes in the area of Malton, and not whether it is the cheapest which we can get. I have already heard disturbing rumours that the next phase of this plane selection, that is, the contract phase, is not due to start until the middle of January. I ask the minister if he cannot wring a decision out of the cabinet to approve the short list and get on with the next stage now, rather than two months from now. It is my understanding that this would enable the final choice and final contract to be signed some four to five months from the start of the contract phase. If this is correct, and I am not certain that it is, that would enable the final decision and the final contract to be signed in the very early spring, perhaps as early as March.
I make this suggestion in the hope that the matter of partisan politics can be kept out of this, and, of course, it will be impossible if the final selection is to be made during the election campaign. Only the Prime Minister knows when the election campaign will be, but we know the date by which we are certainly going to have one. It seems to me that it would be politically immoral for this decision to be postponed for partisan political advantage and then brought up in the middle of a political campaign, to say nothing of the fact that it is also considered politically immoral to make a major commitment just before an election. I make this suggestion in all sincerity, that the government should attempt very hard to make a decision and have the contract signed by the end of March, because it would then avoid being accused of doing it for political purposes. If it cannot come to a decision by that time, it should guarantee that it will put the matter on the shelf and have it dropped during the campaign period. This would at least give us the hope of coming up with the best, plane most suited for Canadian needs.
I would like to move now to the situation in what used to be known as the Canadian army. The present situation of the land forces, or the army, is compounded by shortages of both manpower and equipment. It has suffered most from the cuts in defence since the present Prime Minister took office. For example, in 1965 the army had 48,000 personnel, and it has
27,000	today, of which only 17,000 are assigned to Mobile Command. No element within the army has been harder hit than the infantry. Even within the last four years the infantry has been cut back from 7,500 to approximately 6,500. No army in the world can retain high morale or remain efficient if there is such a continuous loss of manpower, especially in what is referred to as the teeth arms.
However, the loss in manpower is matched by the fact that the army has very little modern equipment when compared

with either our allies or our potential adversaries. For example, the government has ordered new tanks, but has bought the Leopard one, a tank whose basic design is now 13 years old. The reason that this is significant is that all other countries which operate tanks are moving very rapidly to a new generation of tanks, with bigger guns, improved engines, and the new "Chobham" armour which protects them from the anti-tank missiles with which most Warsaw pact infantry units are now equipped. It is rather daft to ignore the fact that a new generation of tanks will have new guns, new engines, and new armour. If you take those three things away you do not have much tank left.
The other disturbing aspect of the tank purchase is the very small quantity involved. We are replacing more than twice the number of old Centurion tanks with a total of 128 Leopard ones. Under present plans we will have only 78 based in Europe, of which a third are to be held in reserve. This will be our total contribution to NATO's tank forces, which face some
27,000	Warsaw pact tanks on the central front of Europe alone.
Another example is that when Canadian forces are committed to peacekeeping operations, they frequently find that either or both the parties they are trying to keep apart, as well as other elements of the peacekeeping force, carry personal weapons or small arms which are more modern and sophisticated than any possessed by Canadian troops. It should be a sobering thought to realize that our fellow peacekeepers in the Middle East, Ghanaian or Nigerian troops, now have better small arms than the Canadian Armed Forces.
I would now like to talk about the financial support that this government has promised but not delivered to the Armed Forces. The present minister inherited from his predecessor a commitment by the government to, at long last, begin re-equipping the forces. This was the "Richardson formula" whereby the capital budget would be increased by 12 per cent per year in real terms for five years, and the whole of the defence budget would be inflation proofed. The former minister achieved this in 1977-78.
After only one year the present minister voluntarily gave up almost 80 per cent of the promised real growth in the capital budget, and now under the government's restraint program the minister has apparently forgone another $150 million out of his budget. Whichever part of it he has surrendered, he will either be losing the inflation proofing, or yet more from his capital budget. In either case we have had more slippage away from the Richardson formula, which was the minimum necessary to maintain the viability of the forces in the long run.
Just the other day the minister took great umbrage in reply to a question of mine, when I said that they had not increased the budget by 12 per cent. I would like to read to hon. members a few words from the minutes of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence on March 12, 1978, when we were studying the estimates for the Department of National Defence. I asked the associate deputy minister of finance in the Department of National Defence, Mr. Davies:
November 21, 1978

-tell us exactly how much the percentage increased, the real growth percentage increased, in the capital budget this year after you had deducted the $60 million?
Mr. Davies replied:
Mr. Chairman, I believe that worked out... to 2.8 per cent.
I said:
What a come-down from the 12 per cent that everybody expected. So it was actually the inflation rate plus 2.8 per cent.
Mr. Davies replied:
That is the way it worked out, sir.
Notwithstanding the fact that they had just broken the promise to increase the capital budget by 12 per cent in real terms, the minister and the Prime Minister attended a NATO meeting at which they made a second pledge, that they would increase the Canadian defence budget by 3 per cent in real terms per annum overall, so that the alliance's long-term defence program for the next decade could be meaningful, since the alliance pledged itself to do more than just maintain existing levels of spending. This promise, too, they had no sooner made than, in effect, they broke it. Already our annual increase for NATO purposes is down to 2 per cent, and this is only the first year of the program.
In both cases the present minister has used the device of pretending that his formulae are intact, money that he has not got, or he has agreed to give up, he insists is still there-in some heavenly treasury board no doubt, and he goes around the country claiming 12 per cent real growth for the capital budget. The particular ministerial fantasy which permits him to offer this piece of double talk is the so-called, and infinitely flexible, capital envelope. It is a concept which allows a minister to convert a 12 per cent real growth each year into 2 per cent or perhaps 5 per cent, and then at some future date- no doubt when the lions of the Treasury Board lie down with the ministerial lamb of National Defence-the minister of defence says he will get what is owing to him.
This talk of an envelope is simply a cheap political way of changing a definite commitment in the estimates into a political promise. If the minister is allowed to get away with this and the Prime Minister in his backing of it, no doubt we will soon be hearing that the redevelopment of Toronto harbour is still in the envelope, and that the replacement of the weather ship Estevan on the west coast is still in an envelope, although, I believe, the promise is now more than eight years old. We might even hear that the Prince Edward Island causeway is still in some envelope in some remote corner of some department. We are supposed to be happy with these and other statements of the minister.
With his characteristic urge to please, the minister does neither the forces nor the country any service when he continually makes promises which he knows he cannot keep. As well he has a penchant for slight exaggeration. For example, as recently as October 5, 1978, the minister addressed the Men's Canadian Club of Winnipeg. He said the following:
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
We will spend another $700 million this year on orders to replace equipment grown obsolete during years of austerity.
I should like to refer to page 15-12 of the 1978-79 estimates of the Department of National Defence. Under capital of the department, there is a grand total of $685,207,000. Of this amount, construction and acquisition of land, buildings and equipment totals $94,026,000; utilities, materials and supplies, $7 million; professional and special services, $19 million. Clearly the grand total is approximately $150 million less than the minister said would be spent on equipment this year.
With each year that the defence budget fails to get funds promised to it, which are the foundation for buying equipment for the next 15 years, the prospects of the new fighter and ship programs become grimmer. The compounding effect is completely lost, if the defence budget does not get the 12 per cent each year. One does not need more than a basic grasp of arithmetic to see that, unless increases come through now, the necessary base for later expansion will not exist. Without an expansion, obviously it is impossible to buy $2.3 billion worth of fighters, which the minister promised, and $1.5 billion worth of ships, expressed in 1977 dollars, just to name the two largest purchases, unless one stretches the programs and the envelope to the turn of the century. If these programs are delayed that long, it will be impossible for the Armed Forces to meet their existing commitments, simply because long before then the forces will lack basic equipment to do the job.
It is hard news to have to tell the people of the country the situation regarding the re-equipment program. This kind of factual reporting would come better from the minister, but if he is unwilling to come clean with Canadians about the financial jiggery-pokery which is going on with the estimates and budgets of the Department of National Defence, then someone has to do it. As I said earlier in my speech, the bitter truth is that we went for ten years without giving our forces the support which was absolutely necessary for them if they were to carry out the roles assigned to them. Now we must pay. During the next ten years we will have to pay for 20 years of defence expenditures, yet the government indicates its clear unwillingness to tackle the job.
I should like to compare the present situation with the past one in this regard. If we take the figures of the Maritime Command, the Mobile Command and the Air Command, and then add the unallotted troops on a prorated basis, we find that in 1965 the navy had 19,613 men and women and in 1978 it had 16,994; the Mobile Command has gone from 46,000 down to 27,000; and Air Command has gone down from 48,000 to
35,000.	Since 1965 the navy has lost 14 per cent, the army 42 per cent, and the air force 27 per cent.
I hope the minister will take my suggestion about moving on as quickly as possible with the selection of a new fighter aircraft. Last week I was surprised to note that along with the discord which has existed always in the government, the Prime Minister talked about defence equipment at his press conference. He made a very curious comment which did not seem to be noticed by too many people. He referred to the selection of

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mrs. Holt
fighter aircraft and whether it would be cheap or expensive. He said the following:
Well, that's a trade-off that DND will have to advise us on. There are cheaper aircraft of which you can get a greater number for the same price. But, obviously, they are not as good as the more expensive aircraft. And, what they are doing now is the same kind of operation they did when we bought a billion dollars worth of long-range patrol aircraft a couple of years ago. They had to choose between the Boeing which in terms of number of hours flight and so on was a bit better but so much more costly than the Lockheed that they could get more of the Lockheed to do the job and they chose the latter.
Clearly this implies that the Prime Minister thought the Boeing 707 would make a better long-range patrol aircraft. This is totally at variance with what the previous minister of national defence told us, as well as everyone else in the services.
In closing, I suggest the government should get its act together. It should move ahead quickly with this new fighter purchase. We should get it out of the way before the election campaign starts. Let us give the forces the support they richly deserve. Our party believes that they deserve this new fighter aircraft. Our party is in favour and has supported the government in its re-equipment program. We believe that the forces need to be a bit larger. We hope to have the support of other parties in this respect when we are in government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to support the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), a sensitive, responsive Canadian whom I respect very much.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I respect him not only for what he is today, but for his great record of service to Canada since he came here from St. Maurice in 1963. I recall talking to him about Canada, and as no other Canadian he made me understand the depth of love of Canada by French Canadians. He told me his story, and I passed it on to my constituents on the opposite edge of Canada, 4,000 miles from his home, in order to explain the richness and love which bind us as a nation.
The minister's family settled in Lower Canada 325 years ago. The Chretiens fought beside the English in the battle of Chateau Gai in October, 1813, when the Americans invaded Canada. In a private conversation with me, the minister said this:
That is the way it will be today if Rene Levesque tries to break us apart; we French and English will be together.
When he came here in 1963 from his riding of St. Maurice, he was unable to speak a word of English. He had no choice; he had to learn English. It is characteristic of this great and spiritually rich Canadian that he did not resent it. He said it simply: "That was the way it was".
To think that today, in this most complex of duties in Canadian affairs, he is so competent in both languages that he can handle himself articulately, and courteously, in responding to an English member in English and a French member in French!
He is a true federalist. I recall one day when were talking about possible separation, he said:
This is all my Canada. I worked for the north for six years.
He was referring to the time when he was Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
He continued, saying:
Nobody is going to say that is not my north or your north. Nobody is going to split it away or any part of my Canada away and turn the north into a Kuwait for about 60,000 people. My kids and every Canadian's kids ha^e a right to everything that is Canadian.
Let us hope that there will be a spread throughout Canada of this example. It must have been a difficult decision, one of compelling duty, which convinced him to take on his present job. Of course his present job is one that only can cause him grief and be a political nightmare because of the economic crisis and social turmoil throughout the world. He took the job when others quit. Let us hope this love and duty to Canada in the hearts of the Chretiens, many Anglophones and others of many cultures-a mix which makes Canada such a magnificent nation-will shame and quiet the hatemongers, those few who spew out their intolerance and irrational hate.
It is love and mutual respect between people which will keep us strong against all divisive forces, some of which are right in the House and up in "yon Fourth Estate."
1 want to speak of the need of excellence in communication, the importance of the media as a responsible public utility, although in private hands, and the importance of an informed and wise electorate as fundamental to a healthy democracy. Conversely, if there is a dearth of responsible and fair reporting, as seems to be the case in Canada, democracy will fail and the first victims always will be the symbol of all freedoms, the free press.
Tragically, communication lines across the land have become warped and distorted. In fact there seems to be a concerted effort to keep honest and fair communication down to a minimum. It seems, as Thomas I. Emerson in his book "The System of Freedom of Expression" has stated, that the most formidable threat to freedom of the press comes less from government than from the media itself. Professor Emerson, who was a law professor at Yale, put it this way:
-that it is no longer to protect the freedom of the press from government interference in order to guarantee freedom of expression. Today, "the overpowering monopoly over the means of communication acquired by the mass media" constitutes the "most significant threat" to our system of freedom of expression.
This country has been well managed. The results are discussed internationally with respect and with admiration. We should all be proud of the international recognition that we are receiving right now.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This government-it is recognized throughout the industrial world-has given us the highest standard of living in the world, but few in the media are telling it. Praise in the international economic community for Canada's leader-

November 21, 1978

ship, compared to the carping at home, proves the old truism-the prophet is without honour in his own country. Canada's economic record is excellent according to an independent assessment made by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, which is composed of 15 of the most industrialized nations in the world, of which Canada is one. These are countries with which we do 90 per cent of our trade.
Another independent voice that recognized Canada's position objectively is that of Earle McLaughlin, chief executive of the Royal Bank of Canada. He claims that in the past seven years Canada has outperformed the Americans by almost any economic yardstick. In that period, real personal incomes in Canada increased 38 per cent, even taking into account the weakened dollar. Compare that to our great neighbour to the south, which had an increase of 17 per cent. Mr. McLaughlin said that Canada's material standard of living increased more than that of the United States, and despite unemployment he notes that Canada has led the world in creating new jobs. We have done better than the second best, which is the United States, having created 50 per cent more jobs than the Americans.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Total investment spending in Canada also rose, according to Mr. McLaughlin. He would be interested in that fact, and so should the Conservatives because he is their man. It rose by 168 per cent, compared with 107 per cent in the United States.
Dr. Carl Beigie, the highly respected economist, author, teacher of managerial economics at McGill University, and president of the C. D. Howe Institute, which like himself is proudly non-partisan and objective, analysed the Canadian economic record at a breakfast meeting I attended, along with others, sponsored by Reader's Digest, on October 31. He said that Canada has as sound a medium-term economic strategy in terms of its fundamentals as any industrialized nation in the world. He goes on to say that there have been tactical errors but that this is virtually inevitable in the real world of political economy. Anyone who imagines that we who live in a narrow belt stretching 4,000 miles across this land can solve all of the world's problems is a dreamer and not very realistic.
We in Canada did very well despite a decade in which there was a shocking upheaval in world economies, where the wealth and control of energy resources shifted from the traditional power areas into the hands of a few sheiks and dictators via a third world cartel. It was a transfer of economic power that set off a tidal wave of inflation in 1973 through the OPEC cartel's fabricating of an energy crisis and then overnight quadrupling the price of oil, and thus energy prices.
But despite all this the record from OECD shows that we survived and came out of it at the top of the economic scale. Our standard of living improved continuously. A recent OECD study ranked Canada second in quality of life among the 15 most industrialized countries. Our GNP increased 32 per cent in real terms. Personal disposable income grew 118 per cent.
The Budget-Mrs. Holt
Average family income went up 35 per cent in real terms. Our 1973-76 growth rate of 9.9 per cent ranked us third in the western world. Our job creation rate of 8.8 per cent-that is,
250,000	jobs a year-between 1973 and 1976 was the highest in the world. Our export trade grew dramatically, with a record trade surplus of close to $3 billion in 1977. Private sector capital investment has run at about 22 per cent a year, compared to 14 per cent in the United States. Second quarter corporate earnings for 1978 are up 20 per cent over 1977. There are now 36 companies with sales of over $1 billion, six more than in 1977.
The whole world has been struck by spiralling inflation with economic stagnation. High unemployment has resulted as long used economic procedures failed to produce expected solutions. Who would be so childlike in the adult world here and in the media as to expect Canada to remain immune to the ailments of the entire world? Here we had virtually economic primitives controlling and manipulating the sophisticated industrialized nations, and the adolescents in the media-yes, even here in the highest institution in the nation-expect classic, old style results from old style procedures.
Listening to some members here and seeing the messages going out throughout Canada, one would think that 264 people, members of parliament, representing 22 million constituents living in a narrow band stretched across 4,000 miles along the 49th parallel, as I mentioned, would alone be able to solve the problems that beset the world. It is less than genius to pretend that Canada alone can solve these problems. One can only assume that the critics are either dishonest or stupid. To be charitable, one might suggest they are sincere but naive-a terribly dangerous combination.
One has to wonder if contemporary rules of journalism proscribe that positive news must never be reported, that the public must be harangued into an intense anxiety state by the unending barrage of cliches and verbiage that threaten the end of the good life. Sometimes we who sit here have the feeling that the news is bringing us to the edge of the world. But it is all too often that this brand of reportage as projected, not the reality or the facts, provides the basis for public anger, unrest, frustration and terrible anxiety. We members of parliament, regardless of our politics, must share in this and possibly in the destruction of our own parliament.
One must wonder if the reasoning behind this is so superficial and selfishly petty as to be ludicrous. Is it fear by media "stars" that their personal status as pundits will be threatened? The Fourth Estate, as we call it here, though it hardly deserves that name until it returns to the style by which it earned that magnificent title-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What would you call it, then?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My colleague asks me what I would call it. It is still the Fourth Estate in world affairs. If the Fourth Estate were doing its job it would have a right to claim its status as the fourth and greatest estate in a free society. But do some members of this Fourth Estate fear that their personal status as pundits is threatened? If their predictions of disaster and
1332

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mrs. Holt
tragedy fail to materialize, it would be a personal blow to their small egos. They would find themselves going nowhere. What an irresponsible influence on Canadian democracy-on the need for a well informed electorate to select an excellent parliament and to structure a healthy nation.
I want to say that there are still high calibre reporters here. I could name them, but time does not permit it. Surely it is to the critical and large public utility that we must direct our attention. The monopoly owners must certainly look to what is happening here before it gets even further out of hand. The owners are fourteen men-all men, and maybe that is the problem. There are fourteen owners of the major communication media in this country. Montreal and West, the English media of every major city is controlled by three companies, Southam's, F.P. Publications, and the Thomson group. These three companies unify to tell us and tell Canada what is happening. They do not have to be honest, they do not have to face the checks of competition; they do not have to do anything but manipulate and control this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is the same thing in New Brunswick.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is just what I was going to say. East of Montreal it is the K.C. Irving group. It should be cause for fear for all of us. If they can divide this House they can conquer this House. They-those 14-will be the people who will be running Canada, if they are not already.
I say that the media has the most important duty of any profession in any free country. It is truly the most crucial agency for strength or for destruction.
For democracy to flourish it must have a free, responsible, fair, balanced and, most important, an accurate press.
The right of the public to know is the highest principle of a free society. The people who tout this the loudest today on this hill are the very people who use self-serving censorship-the media. Those of us who despise the secrecy that allows bullies and sadists to flourish within the public service feel that it is essential to have openness and that the public has a right to know. But it seems that this right to know in Canada gets mixed with the right of some journalists here to use their own so-called discretion as to what the public should be told. The distortion and censorship that are flourishing in this country have been described as one of the most "formidable threats" to society today. That is by Emerson and by other great leaders in both the United States and in Canada. It is as though the right to know must be submerged to the right to keep good news secret. It is as though the truth may spoil the fiction.
I recall following the appearance of the RCMP before our justice committee, about a year ago, when many accusations and so-called scandals were explained, even explained away by the RCMP commissioner on a morning show. It was a national network but I will not name it. The commissioner gave the answers to our committee. The interviewer, noted as much for his accusative style of telling facts as for questioning, got

responses he obviously did not like. They answered the charges and exploded media scandal stories. The answers left the interviewer with egg on his face. He whined on the air publicly, "But that spoiled my story."
Recently, on this same show the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais), being interviewed regarding cabinet ministers' appearances before the McDonald inquiry into the RCMP, said the ministers want to be heard in public. Minutes later, on the news, the story was sent across Canada that the Solicitor General wanted to appear in camera. I could not believe this was possible in a free and open society.
Another trick that hon. members opposite will know as well as we do is the "voice-over" technique. If the speaker is telling something and saying it well, making a forceful argument- whether it is the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-they use voice-over and translate it the way they want, not necessarily telling what was said.
During the federal-provincial conference it was remarkable that the two pinch-hitters for CBC told of an end to the conference of discord between the first ministers of the provinces and the Prime Minister. People who watched it live saw the conference as it really ended. They also heard B.C. premier Bill Bennett and other first ministers talk of it as a successful up-beat conference. These realities inspired one caller to an open line show, in which I participated in Vancouver, to ask, "Does the CBC executive censor truth?"

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What does Allan Fotheringham know about Canada anyway?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He reports from Vancouver about Ottawa-a
3,000	mile perspective of Ottawa.
Donald McDonald, editor of the respected Centre Magazine, November-December, 1976, pages 15 to 35, sets out the duty of the media this way:
The premise of democracy is that a people can govern themselves. The condition for this audacious assumption is that the people will have the information they need to make wise political decisions. Democracy, the philosopher Richard McKeon has pointed out, is a community based on communication. Judge Learned Hand has said that we have staked our all on the rational dialogue of an informed electorate.
Mr. McDonald said, and I agree, that the press, that is, broadcasting and print, as the chief medium of communication among people and for people, remains the most effective way to relay what is happening. He says that they have betrayed the greatest duty of one of the most important professions for a strong nation.
These are such exciting and challenging times for great communicators, not only because of the subject matter that changes so quickly, but because of the availability of the tiniest and most colorful events in every corner of the world through jet travel and space communication. Today we have spectacular devices for instant communication and for visual experiences in every home-not just television but satellite, bringing instantaneous information from all corners of the earth. The public that has invested so much in this, and has a right to
November 21, 1978

expect so much, is being cheated. It is a critical, distrustful public, frustrated, betrayed, resenting the fact that it cannot rely on the printed word or even the voices on radio or pictures on their television screens.
The people are seeking information but cannot find an information source they can trust. The public today is not what the media were told 30 or 40 years ago-of an average mentality of fourteen years; the public today is educated and wise, perhaps much, much wiser than those in the media who are not classed, by law, as professionals.
We hear talk of paranoia. When the media is told that there is something wrong, something out of joint in the composition of its membership, they cannot think or talk about anything else but their hurt feelings. Their minds blot out everything else, all real news that affects the people of Canada. All their energy and thought are focussed on their own insult. Many know it is true. But nothing else matters, it is their ox that is gored. They become angry and dangerous, typical of paranoia. The killer instinct is the result of much paranoia. I would not be surprised if it is paranoia-schizophrenia, because many of them do not know what they are yet. I want to say that there are great exceptions.
The Prime Minister said that the media is the enemy. It is regrettable that they do not give equal attention to the Prime Minister's general statements, for example, that of October 12 in this House which was an important report to the people of Canada on the positive state of the nation.
Unfortunately the group, in the media, engaging in this paranoid-killer journalism, too lazy to do any investigative work, are wallowing in their own ego trips and giving a bad name to a great profession. The behaviour of this group ruins the responsible, fair job of reporting being done by others. It is tragic that this is happening, and nobody regrets it more than those of us who want to see a competitive press, a press that is rich and objective.
There is no doubt that the government must look into the whole business-another aspect of the press-of monopoly, and move toward an anti-trust type of legislation to restore healthy competition, to allow comparisons and force the industry out of sloth into the high standards that such comparison and competition impose.
It is also essential for the government to look into the power broking within its own agency, the CRTC, that has abused its mandate and is usurping power of parliament, diminishing competition in the electronic media and, worst of all, bullying the public and depriving the citizens of freedom of choice and freedom to have the best and most varied choices on which to base their knowledge and information.
The government must also review the CBC role as it lives off the public purse. It is costing the taxpayers more than a half a billion dollars a year to get distorted, biased, irresponsible information, in the name of national culture. The CBC had four cameras in the rotunda on budget night with which to
The Budget-Mrs. Holt
do a poorer job than the other two networks-CTV and Global-did with one camera each.
Incidentally, the waste to Canadian taxpayers by an Ottawa bureau chief, who may have a serious conflict of interest in pushing his personal political interests on the Canadian public, must also be checked. I am surprised that the media never write about this type of thing. I would also like to know why we had all that equipment out on the hill for three weeks pushing for an election. Maybe someone should look into that. I notice the whip on the other side knows what I am talking about. And one member of the Fourth Estate in the press gallery, now. Congratulations to that member-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Everybody is watching it on TV.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I said, it is the lazy way of doing it. They cannot see all the great things that you people are doing across the room or here if they sit and watch it on television.
Referring to responsible journalists, they are more important than the media charlatans in Canadian democratic life. None are more worried about the situation than the responsible journalists in Canada and the United States. Wherever these people meet, they talk of their fears and of what is happening to their profession and to the country because of the cretins.
Concerning the media's self-serving censorship, I would refer to a statement made by law professor Stephen R. Barnett of the University of California in Berkley, which appeared in 1973 in an article in The Nation. It reads:
The media tend to look the other way on important issues in which they-and perforce the public-are involved.
"One hears much about reporters' subpoenas and the threat they pose to the public's right to know, but considerably less about other controversies involving the media, the government, and the First Amendment. . . The whole subject of media concentration somehow eludes the nation's newspapers and TV stations. Two years ago, for example, when Congress made its own contribution to newspaper monopoly by passing the Newspaper Preservation Act, the publishers' lobbying campaign was backed up by studied blandness in the nation's press ... Last summer, when the industry took another major step toward monopoly by killing major newspapers in Boston, Washington, and Newark, the help provided by the justice department was overlooked in the media. At present, the leading nonstory is the proposal of the Federal Communications Commission to break up common ownership of newspapers and broadcast stations in cities throughout the country-an uncommonly important and controversial issue that may be unrivaled for the thoroughness with which the media have blacked it out."
We have the same mergers, we have the same monopoly development, we have the same control, and we have the same irresponsibility of which Professor Barnett speaks. Is anyone reporting these developments? What about the takeover of newspapers by management groups, for example, F.P. Publications? The Globe and Mail was taken over by F.P. Publications and it deteriorated. Nobody has written about why that happened. It is essential now for Canada to halt and reverse this dangerous concentration of ownership by fewer and fewer people. The media character of the 1970s-neither technologically or structurally-could have been foreseen by the Fathers of Confederation when they planned this great democracy. They could not have foreseen what it would mean to a self-governing society spread across this massive land, that
80067-13%

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mrs. Holt
could not hear or know what was happening in its capitals, both provincial and federal, and even in municipal councils, because of deliberate distortion and evasion of truth.
McDonald in the Centre Magazine also notes two characteristics that bear most heavily on the performance of working journalists and the quality of public reporting. First is the big business nature of the media; and second is the increasing concentration of their ownership in fewer and fewer hands. Both jeopardize the freedom and diversity of expression.
Therefore they make problematic the possibility of realsitic and wise decision-making by the Canadian people. That is why Canadians are only listening to the stories of crepe hanging, the stories of doom, the stories of fear and the hate that have spread across this land from parliament. It affects not just the Government of Canada but everyone.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to inform the hon. lady that her allotted time has expired. She may continue with unanimous consent. Is there unanimous consent?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think we all have to worry about the division and contempt that the whole of this parliament is feeling.
In an American Press interview 13 years ago Walter Lipp-man said:
A free press exists only where newspapers, which are competitive and rivals, exist, so that editorial comment and news reports can-regularly and promptly-be compared, verified and validated. A press monopoly is incompatible with a free press.
Nobody wants great journalism, great reporting, and great Canadiana more than great journalists want it. All who are confident in their own ability and have integrity want to compete in the largest markets.
Most good writers and artists try for the best and do not want to succeed in sheltered workshops. Only mediocrity and incompetence seek protection from competition. This hardly makes the nation better or provides an informed electorate. The one thing we must all worry about is an informed public. It affects everyone and democracy itself.
When the election was called in 1974, the monopoly press of Vancouver, which exists in every major city of Canada, called a meeting of the top executives of the Vancouver Province and the Vancouver Sun. These papers did not have to compete, so their representatives decided how to do the job on the cheap. A think tank was organized to decide how they would cover the election. Only the leaders got coverage, which meant the electorate of British Columbia went to the polls without knowing the strengths, weaknesses or the positions of the candidates for whom they had to vote.
If parliament is to have strength, and democracy is to survive, there must be an informed public and a responsible media.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for the new member for St. Boniface to deliver his first speech in the House and that it should be about the budget. Allow me to say, Mr. Speaker, that the fact that I have remained quiet for days while the other new members have already delivered their speech does not mean that I will remain so in the future. It must be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that my predecessor is the senator from St. Boniface, Mr. Joseph-Phillippe Guay, and my performance must be better than his own. However, at this time I want to pay him a tribute and say that during my two election campaigns, I have noted how well known and admired he was by every resident of St. Boniface.
Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious that I am older than the other new members in the House. Indeed, I belong to the generation of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I am also a grandfather.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear. And my neighbour too.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that is right. I would also like to tell you a very short story to explain why I speak like the member from-

-"the safest Liberal seat in the west".
My background has been primarily in the food and agricultural industry. Although I began many years ago in the academic and scientific research field, most of my 20 years in business has been in management, particularly in the budgetary and sales aspects of marketing.
After many years in the pharmaceutical, food and grain industry, I started my own business in agribusiness consulting. Our offices have been in the Winnipeg Grain Exchange for the past eight years. Our clientele has included food processing, chemical, and agricultural supply companies.
I represent a very small company. The employees are nonunion. Although much of our work is in consulting, we are involved in sales of ingredients and inputs for the feed and farm industry.
Early in the 1970s when I started my own business we were going along rather smoothly, but shortly I found there was a rapid increase of government intervention. This involvement appeared to increase from year to year. We had more and more forms to fill out. There were more taxes to pay. It reached the point where our little company had the honour of having our own financial inspection of the books by government accountants, and that was a two week stint.
We noted a growing number of government offices surrounding us in the Grain Exchange. There were two floors of
November 21, 1978

Manpower offices. Ministry of Transport people appeared on all sides. None of these people appeared to be working very hard with their long coffee breaks and long lunch hours. We noticed this as we were hurrying from one appointment to the other.
At the same time, the government was encroaching into individuals' lives more and more. The very size of government increased all around us. Taxes kept going up to the point where I felt I was carrying the whole load of government on my shoulders.
At this time, in the early days of his mandate, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) philosophized that if a person did not want to work, we really ought not force him to do so against his will, and so was born the costly social programs of the late sixties and early seventies such as LIP, YIP and other giveaway programs. The role of unemployment insurance was no longer insurance as we know it, but in fact high level welfare. Young persons were given to feel that the money tree was there for the picking. My own sons, growing through their teens, told me of schemes whereby they could detour around work and still live rather well. Hon. members can rest assured that they were given short shrift by me with those ideas.
Along with this government intervention, other aspects of the economy were making me queasy. There appeared to be little forward planning by government, and the Auditor General inferred that the government was losing control over its spending. Inflation and unemployment seemed to rocket upwards.
At about that stage, with all those indicators giving me strong nudges, an otherwise apolitical businessman became fed up to the teeth. I felt that the younger generation was quickly losing the finer spirit that our forefathers needed to hew out their livelihood in the Canadian wilds, yet Canada possessed unlimited undeveloped resources, resources that would require a heavy dose of the old pioneer spirit, both physically and mentally, to bring them to market stages.
Here was a country with a paucity of population relative to size, lands as yet unexplored, and it was regressing into a country that within a short while would be unable to carry out its own development, all because of the application of artificial socialistic strategy. We needed that pioneer spirit and the rugged determined character in our young folks in order to maximize our potential. It was my feeling that as the character of the young people went, so would go our country.
I well knew that one person could not make much impression on the total process, so the next step was taken, involvement in the political process. To keep the story short, we did not make much headway in the 1974 election.
