However, in 1978 with tremendous effort by a lot of people and a fast running campaign, we presented the viable alternative to the citizens of federal St. Boniface in the hastily called six weeks by-election.
Such an upset as was achieved, along with the other nine by-election wins, I believe justified my position as a candidate for the past five years. At least I know that the voice of the
The Budget-Mr. Hare
people is truly being heard throughout the land. Come next summer, the final awakening of the Canadian public will occur.
Since my background is in business, particularly business management, I state here that the present management practices of government as shown in the recent budget are deplorable.

Mr. Speaker, the reason for my intervention is that I think sound and generally accepted management principals should be applied in a country such as Canada. Without sound management, a company cannot be viable nor progress. Any profitable company establishes its objectives and a plan for action well before proceeding with each phase of both shortterm and long-term development. Its marketing plan is complete and is prepared with all details including time and financial indicators. That is the practical application of the concept of marketing. This concept does not relate only to products for sale but to the whole process of production, transformation, transportation, promotion and to the economic factors or, in other words, to the planning process as a whole. The idea is to direct the various products towards the appropriate markets. It implies the analysis of potential markets as well as the internal movement of all information.

The budget brought down this week again illustrates the poor management abilities of the present government. As a businessman I can say there are many key problems under our present economic conditions that the budget did not touch. I would like to relate these briefly and present some of the reasons why they have not been taken care of now.
The first is the high cost of money. As a small businessman, this affects the development of my company and my ability to obtain working capital. Second is the impact of unemployment insurance and its effect on the high turnover rate of labour at the lower levels. It is almost impossible to get and maintain working people. Third, there is a lack of high quality and skilled labour. Fourth, there is a lack of incentives for entrepreneurial action. There is very little reason for me, as a small businessman, to keep on going, encourage larger growth, and continue to pay taxes, when I could do almost as well by taking a government job or going on welfare.
The whole thing has resulted in lack of confidence in the government because of its short-term, band-aid, month to month policies. All these things are adding to the cost of production and limiting our ability to produce low cost products allowing us to compete in the domestic and international marketplace.
Let me apply some of my thinking to an area with which I am more familiar-the food and agricultural sector. There are many things wrong in this area in Canada and I would like to point out a few items, and perhaps in future debates get down to detail. One of the greatest impacts on our cost of living is

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Hare
the price of food. Everyone is hit hard when food prices rise. Thus the optimization of our food industry is essential if we are to have any aptitude in the maintenance of low food prices. The fact that Canada is so large makes the transportation of our food products an important aspect of cost. Yet I see many things which make me shudder when I review the food policies in effect at this time. This is particularly true of my own location, the prairies and western Canada. I wish to refer briefly to a few instances but I shall not take the time to go into detail.
I refer to improprieties which relate to our high cost of food. Optimum management would not allow such things to occur resulting in the poor situation which exists in our economy. First, I would turn to the grain movement process. In the normal elevators of western Canada we have almost no cleaning operations in the prairies. Only in the newer and larger elevators do we find grain cleaning facilities. Thus the dockage or screenings which in some cases amount to some 15 or 20 per cent of crops such as rapeseed is shipped from the prairies to storage elevators in Vancouver, Thunder Bay, Prince Rupert or Churchill, where the grain is cleaned to international specifications. This represents a waste of transportation capacity at a time when railway cars are in short supply, and adds substantially to costs.
As to livestock production, I find that when I speak about agriculture in western Canada people in the east are astonished by how things progress. First we grow calves in B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and ship them to the eastern provinces. Then we grow feed grains-barley, wheat, etc.-on the prairies and then ship these crops to eastern locations. Farmers in eastern locations then raise calves for beef production using western grain. When one considers the shortage of transportation and the high cost of transportation, this is certainly not an economical process to follow.
I briefly mention the quota aspect of grain production. Under our Canadian system the average increase in wheat yield per acre has only been fractional over the past 25 to 50 years. On the other hand, corn production in the United States under the open market system has increased by four times. The potential for grain production in western Canada has only started. If we were able to optimize productivity by more intensive farming, our production could increase by a factor of two, three or four.
Another area in which the economy has gone awry is in the export of our commodities. Canada over many years has been an exporter of commodities. Why is this so? We ship raw grain, minerals, coal etc. out of Canada when we should be doing the processing and developing our industries, particularly secondary industries, on the prairies.
I would like now to pay attention to my own constituency of St. Boniface where there are many problems, some of which have to do with its particular relationship to the city of Winnipeg. It is also true, as I have heard stated here, that where there are problems there are opportunities. St. Boniface is one of the largest feed and livestock manufacturing areas of western Canada. Why then are we losing some of our meat

packing industry to the east? Why is it that although we have some of the cheapest land in Canada for the production of agricultural products, our livestock production is not increasing in the way it should? Why is food production going out of the west where it can be produced at the least cost? The marketing programs required for increased sales and production and getting the food industry in the west progressing the way it should are not in place.
I would like to point to the downtown St. Boniface area which, as many hon. members know, is very close to the downtown area of Winnipeg, joined only by one or two bridges. In the downtown centre of Winnipeg the excavation work for the joining of the four corners of Portage and Main will be completed in but a few weeks. About three or four blocks to the east, in St. Boniface, you cross the bridge and enter into what is almost a slum area. The money which has been put into development has been expended on the west side of the Red River. The St. Boniface area is in great need of development if it is to be brought up to standards of manufacturing which it can attain.
The fact that St. Boniface has historically been the site of the greatest French-Canadian culture of western Canada is not being utilized to the best advantage. The old cathedral of St. Boniface, which was burned a few years ago, has been restored to some extent, but the whole area of St. Boniface, with its French flavour, has not reached the potential of which it is capable. There has to be some development to make St. Boniface truly the centre of French Canadian culture in western Canada.
There are two or three industries in my riding to which I should like to pay attention. One of them has been the object of some interest over the past few years. It is the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. I believe all hon. members know there have been many problems in the management of this operation in the past few years. There has been a good deal of fish spoilage in the accumulation process by the Fish Marketing Corporation, resulting in the loss of many hundreds of thousands of dollars. The fishermen are very unhappy at the prices they are receiving, to the extent that some of them are going around the Fish Marketing Corporation and bringing their fish directly into the city of Winnipeg to sell their product. Pickerell is fetching only $1 per pound, whereas on the open market it is selling at $3 and $4 a pound.
I turn now to an important part of western Canada's income earning capacity-the grain industry. Over the past five or six years we have produced many large railway hopper cars to handle grain transportation in western Canada. When I was involved in the 1974 election campaign the government was in the process of looking at this question of hopper cars, and at that time we made a strong point to utilize the CN yards in Transcona as a location for the manufacture of some of these cars. After all, the grain industry is in the west. The locations of these manufacturers of the grain hopper cars, however, are in Ontario, Quebec, and the maritimes. There should be a manufacturing location in western Canada, such as Transcona, which has all of the facilities. There would certainly be some
November 21, 1978

capital involvement, but it would be an ideal site for such an industry to develop, and would establish a firmer base for the CN railway repair program.
In conclusion, I have presented several aspects of the Canadian economy that require better management. There are many others that I have not brought up, but the budget of last week will not solve many of these problems. This budget, like all the recent budgets, is not based on sane, sensible, business oriented decisions. It is more of an after-the-fact budget with all of its band-aid approaches, when major surgery is required. How much longer can the Canadian people endure the arrogance of the present government? How much longer can we stand the flip-flop thinking, as it primarily relates to maintaining the Liberals in power?

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude-Andre Lachance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
By way of an introduction to my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I wish to extend my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) for introducing a budget which, contrary to what some expected and others feared, is a responsible document which reflects the difficult times we are facing, the long term preoccupations in the mind of a minister who does not intend to play tricks on Canadians or make rash promises, the concerns which are based on the extensive consultations which the minister has held with the various levels of activities in Canada, whether with his provincial counterparts, his colleagues in cabinet, the representatives of the money market, the business community, the unions and labour force.
In short, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has again taken steps to consult every productive sector within our society with a view to coming up with a document not only outlining the structural and conjunctural problems faced by our Canadian economy, but also guiding the economy and the economic agents in order that they take a better orientation for the better days which could not but come during the next few months and the next few years. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think the minister must be commended heartily for this budget which, as every commentator pointed out, is an honest and responsible budget showing on the part of the government its intention to accomplish serious things with the economy and also its long term concerns, and in that respect I think the minister must be commended for his budget.
Having said that, I should like to transcend the detailed provisions in the budget, although I will refer to them a little later, to deal with a tremendous problem which is of great concern to me as a member from the province of Quebec; it is the endemic difficulties faced by the Quebec economy over the last fifteen years or so as shown by the gradual but persistent decline of Quebec's share in the Canadian economy and particularly in the manufacturing sector. That situation particular to Quebec, even though it can result from more general
The Budget-Mr. Lachance
problems and from the over-all situation of the Canadian economy, might be more difficult to resolve. It will be difficult to remedy those structural deficiencies only through indicative actions, tax legislation or even monetary policies that can be provided in a budget. Indeed, the government, which is well aware of those problems, has undertaken consultations with all levels of economic activity in an attempt to find solutions to those structural problems, and I will return to that point later.
Coming back to the budget itself, I would simply like to say that, contrarily to what some defenders of extreme expansion or some defenders of extreme restrictions say, the economists, those people who were already watching the economic indicators, were fully aware, even before the budget was tabled, that the Minister of Finance was facing a dilemma. On the one hand, his margin was obviously very narrow; and on the other hand, the Economic Council of Canada and other organizations directly involved in economic issues strongly suggested that the government should continue to emphasize expansion through tax legislation.
I should like to refer to the monthly business review published by the Bank of Montreal for the month of October 1978 in which were pointed out the difficulties which the Minister of Finance met magnificently. I quote:
The government therefore faces a dilemma: a huge dificit, and the need to contain the growth of the money supply in order to resist inflationary pressures, make tax reductions untimely; on the other hand, reducing the tax burden would be desirable to stimulate the economy.
All that to say, Mr. Speaker, that once again the two main opposition parties missed the boat. On the one hand, serving some sort of "pudding" to which we are starting to get used, though I hope Canadians never do, the spokesmen for the official opposition, through an alchemy the recipe for which we have yet to get-and again, I hope they give it to us some day-would like us to both contain expenditures and reduce revenues while stimulating the economy and giving back to private enterprise the role of leader it did not manage to assume in the past; in short, they serve some sort of "pudding" which really defies analysis. Anyway, economic commentators, after the speech of their leader, pointed out all sorts of incongruities which I leave to others the care of analyzing in detail.
On the other hand, we have the spokesmen for the New Democratic Party who, through a turn of mind I cannot fathom either, would have us-and Canadians believe that by stimulating the Canadian economy to death, and in particular, by increasing even more our current budgetary deficit, we could, even over the short term, reduce that deficit within two or three years while at the same time creating employment.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out to you, though you surely are aware of it as well as I am, that this government is concerned about the creation of jobs. It has allocated hundreds

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Lachance
of millions of dollars to this end, and I fail to see how a policy such as the one advocated by the NDP could cure the cyclical problems on the one hand, since these are often beyond our means of action, and on the other hand, and what's more important, cure the structural problems facing the Canadian economy.
Moreover, I would like once again to point out to members of the opposition that they who are changing their tune according to the fashion of the day and especially according to editorials of the day before, should perhaps take a look at the publication prepared by the Economic Council of Canada and entitled Horizon 1982. This document pointed out a number of objectives the government should examine closely in order to find a remedy to these problems they enumerated and that I mentioned before. In particular, it said, and I quote:
In general, we propose that governments should move rather carefully to maintain adequate growth in aggregate demand, while moving more vigorously to encourage needed structural change through incentives and improved mechanisms for consultation on basic economic issues.
The council then gave some recommendations, concerning in particular international competitiveness, which made the government put a lot of emphasis on the promotion of Canadian products in foreign countries, either by the government itself or through trade missions, sometimes under the chairmanship of government officials but also, as in the case of the recent trade mission to China, under the chairmanship and leadership of Canadian industrialists.
I am surprised that some opposition members have denounced this intensive action undertaken, for example, by the Export Development Corporation, whose role is precisely to encourage the development of foreign markets. This recommendation came from the Economic Council of Canada and I think that the government has followed up well on it.
Industrial adaptation, which was the second recommendation formulated by the council is a problem which, once again, is of concern to many Canadians; it concerns industrial markets and the government, I should say governments, since this issue was the subject of two federal-provincial conferences in less than a year, the one in February and the one held last week, and, as I said, I will come back to this problem which is the main topic of my speech today.
Unemployment was the subject of the third recommendation. While the Economic Council itself recognized that it would be extremely difficult to solve this problem unless we completely mess up the economic equilibrium and promote or create galloping inflation by instituting oversized job-creation mechanisms, this very Economic Council however mentioned some regional unemployment disparities which have to be dealt with. In this regard, I quote again its report:
The problem is rendered more difficult by the uneven pace of regional economic growth and the persistence of chronically high unemployment and underemployment in many areas of the Atlantic provinces and Quebec and in the rural and northern regions of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I simply want to indicate that the budget presented by the Minister of Finance contains a provision which should allow us to correct some of the deficiencies identified by the Economic Council, particularly regarding the investment tax credit. I would like to congratulate the minister for having done away with that unhealthy attitude which prevented us from basing our fiscal policies on regional disparities and for having at last allowed for an investment tax credit taking into account the needs of the various areas of the country. These new investments eligible for tax credit generate jobs, and they do; according to the recommendations of the Economic Council this new tax credit will be raised from its present 10 per cent to 20 per cent in the Atlantic provinces and in the Gaspe Peninsula and, under the Regional Development Incentives subsidies will rise from 7.5 per cent to 10 per cent in other designated areas and from 5 per cent to 7 per cent in the other regions.
Mr. Speaker, I think this measure will have very important repercussions on the expansion in those regions that in the past for various reasons did not enjoy the same growth rate as other regions of the country.
I could go on enumerating the recommendations made by the Economic Council of Canada in the publication Horizon 1982 and we would come to the conclusion that, although this council is of course only one adviser to the federal government among many others, it took into consideration views from experts, and without indulging into the excesses suggested on the opposition side whether by the New Democratic Party or by the Progressive Conservative party, succeeded in giving the Canadian economy this growth rate, which, while being clearly slower than expected, brought along an increase in employment which was not sufficient but which was greater than in any other OECD country and could partly dampen the rate of inflation. Members on the opposition side always convey the bad news. I shall simply refer once again to the businesses review of the Bank of Montreal, the document I quoted from earlier which gives the good news for the last few months and which stated in particular that while the rate of unemployment is relatively stable because of the constant increase in inputs, there was a job creation rate of more than 3.5 per cent, which is a very high increase. There was a drop of 1 per cent in the price of food, the over-all index has remained stable since October, the number of housing starts increased to a yearly rate of 225,000, industrial production went up by 1.1 per cent in July, a very high yearly rate of 14 per cent, which brought the index up by at least 5.4 per cent, and so on.
Is this the example of a government announcing the failure of our economy, or rather is this the result of the progressive and reasonable initiatives taken by the government in the last several years to try to make the best out of a situation which is very difficult since it affects the whole world, and more particularly all the industrialized countries? To illustrate this
November 21, 1978

point, I shall simply say that it is not for nothing that the prime ministers of all these countries have gone through the trouble of meeting three times now to attempt to find solutions to these problems, which are not national in scope, but rather international.
Having said this, I would now like to talk about the economic situation in Quebec. As an introduction, I would like to quote a very short article by Michel Belanger, the president and chief executive of the Provincial Bank of Canada, which was published in February 1978 in the publication Commerce. Here is what he said:
The Quebec economy is vulnerable.
The Quebec economy, which is an integral part of the Canadian economy, has evolved more or less at the same pace and its over-all growth this year will probably be about the same as the national average. Of course, we have the same problems as every other area of Canada and our weaknesses are more of a structural nature. The important role of labour intensive consumer goods industries, which are particularly sensitive to wage increases, makes the Quebec economy vulnerable to international market conditions, because to the pressures exerted by labour costs must be added the effect of the lowering of customs duties in accordance with the liberalization of exchange. This is why there have been many layoffs in these sectors.
Mr. Speaker, this problem is very serious, because when we refer to the soft sectors about which there has been a lot of talk recently, especially in view of the problems caused by the provincial sales tax reduction, we are speaking about those sectors which are directly affected on the one hand by the tariff barriers, and on the other hand by the increase in production unit costs, and I am thinking about the textile, clothing, footwear and furniture industries, which play such an important role in the economy of Quebec that if they disappear, hundreds of thousands of jobs will be directly affected.
Mr. Speaker, you will certainly remember that recently, in June 1978, the Economic Council of Canada published a study entitled: Study of Canada relations with developing countries with the following subtitle: For a common future. This is a very disturbing document as it predicts for our future, and not really in the short term but rather in the long term, that those same sectors I just mentioned might soon, in a quickly developed economy like Canada, become a burden that we shall have to carry everywhere in our exchanges with our partners, in multilateral negotiations, in the distribution of investment incentives for Canadian purposes, at the research and development level, and that because of the very nature of those labour intensive industries and also the fact that in developing countries those industries are given the priority as the cost of labour, the production factor, is lower there than in Canada, those industries might considerably suffer from a general industrial development policy on a world wide or Canadian scale and, particularly, in the general context of tariff barriers and tariff reductions.
The Council recommended in that study that:
The federal government should inject a large amount in an industrial adjustment program undertaken in cooperation with concerned provinces, particularly Quebec and Ontario.
Secondly, upon the improvement of the economic situation that might be defined for instance on the basis of an established national unemployment rate
The Budget-Mr. Lachance
level-Canada would phase out the special protection (special quotas and other quantitative restraints on importations) given to vulnerable industries.
Under these two simple recommendations lies a structural revolution of Quebec's economy which has not been matched in recent Canadian history and in that province itself. We are in fact talking about more than 150,000 jobs and the council spoke then about a fund of more than $3 billion which represents a considerable amount of money which had probably prompted the Economic Council to speak then of a healthier economic situation. Without necessarily sharing the views of the council which was taking as its underlying philosophy that in a world scale developmental context more chances would have to be given to the developing countries to build their own economy and to take their place under the sun and that consequently Canada had to give these countries that opportunity by gradually withdrawing from this market in order to concentrate rather on high technology industries, without necessarily completely sharing this philosophy, I repeat, I still consider that very soon, in spite of the fact that preliminary studies have been carried out, and I will come back on that topic, Canada will have to tackle the issue of progressive transfer of resources and means of production of those industries to high technology industries. In order to do so, there will have to be a very strong political will behind this move and there will have to be an understanding on the part of all parties concerned, be they the federal government, the provincial governments and obviously the industry itself. The other Canadian provinces which are less concerned by this problem will have to accept that considerable Canadian resources be rechannelled in order to help in the progressive transfer of the means of production of these industries toward higher technology oriented industries. In short there will have to be a national effort which will require a great resolve on the part of governments concerned.
That moment is getting nearer and nearer. In fact, under the GATT agreement negotiations have taken place to review the whole tariff structure. We have succeeded, Mr. Speaker, in protecting this time again the soft sectors of our industry. The question is whether we will be able to do it in the future when the pressure will become greater on the part of the developing nations on one side and on the other side mainly on the part of the high technology oriented Canadian industries which are now witnessing a drain in their resources and have to face a tariff burden a lot heavier because of these various industries which are asking for a tariff protection which is already very high. I am therefore only raising this issue in order now to deal with what is beginning to happen, what is becoming a common understanding of the different levels of government and what will soon become a more articulated policy.
At the federal-provincial conference in February last, the premiers agreed to ask the federal government to undertake sectoral studies dealing with the main economic activities in Canada. Those 23 studies have enabled us to publish a recent report dated October 15, the so-called Second Tier Report. I would like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that we find in those 23
1340

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Lachance
studies 850 recommendations directed either to the federal government or the provinces and even private entreprise and what is still more interesting, those studies are not merely administrative analyses made by officials, but rather serious concerted efforts of all economic agencies. When the government is accused of doing nothing for the Canadian economy, I am rather shocked that such falsehoods are scattered everywhere.
When we know the government in less than eight or nine months set up 23 multidisciplinary task forces, Mr. Speaker, forced the 23 task forces to submit a report, the recommendations in that report were studied by an over-all committee which submitted a report, when we know that since then there has been a second federal-provincial conference of ministers of industry, is that the mark of a government that is dragging its feet? I cannot believe that! It is rather the mark of a government striving to try and solve the structural problems faced by our Canadian economy.
And we will have to go further that way. Some 450 recommendations were aimed at the national government. A number of them have already been implemented, after a mere few weeks. For example, announcements were made concerning the reduction of red tape. Recommendations concerning research and development are already included in the budget put forward by the Minister of Finance. Fiscal measures were implemented in the same budget concerning both pulp and paper industry and mining. All those recommendations stem from the 23 sectoral studies.
At the same federal-provincial conference, whose thrust was reporting progress, the provinces received the mandate of implementing 200 recommendations in their own jurisdiction. Finally, and perhaps most importantly, private industry itself now has a guideline, because its representatives on the committees developed nearly 200 recommendations to improve productivity and efficiency. And over and above that, Mr. Speaker, I believe we must now to some degree address ourselves to the long term.
If this is a serious effort at restructuring the admittedly ailing Canadian economy, because we never stopped to examine it during the last decades, and my contention is that for the first time a serious effort was made last year to make a general diagnosis of the economy, if we are serious we will have to set up a super-ministry of the economy. We will have to do as the Europeans did after World War II when, faced with the ruins of a devastating war and the prospect of seeing the old pre-war habits set foot again, people with vision like Jean Monnet and others decided it was time for a new departure in the European economy. We have seen that in France, for example, the planning board and other similar bodies have established a system where consultation with various economic agents has been institutionalized in order to modernize the European economy. This is what we need in Canada, Mr. Speaker. Of course, we are not in the same case as Europeans in 1945, 1946 and 1947 who were left in the midst of ruins and rubble.
We have an economy which still works relatively well. But must we wait for this economy to crumble down before taking action or should it not be wiser to detect immediately the cracks, and indeed if we find some faults in this economy why not consolidate immediately the foundations of our industry? I think we should rather follow the second path, Mr. Speaker, as we have seen in the work which has already been done by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce during the federal-provincial conferences which have taken place in February and November, with its various task forces and particularly at all levels of economic activity, at first and second levels. What we need is to carry on acting together and aim at a common goal, in an over-all effort of restructuration.
With this super ministry of the economy, let us call it that way, we could call it a sort of planification board, owing to this super ministry of the economy, Mr. Speaker, we would be able to give an over-all direction and to help various economic agents co-ordinate their efforts which would give our Canadian economy a sound basis for the future.

in this House, some good and a lot more not so good. Let me say that the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) has demonstrated what should be a lesson to a good many of us. His speech showed that he had been doing some reading of the Economic Council of Canada reports, the Bank of Montreal reports, and ITC task force reports. Above all, it showed that he had done some thinking about them and reduced that thinking to some positive ideas and directions that the government should take. On behalf of the ordinary member of parliament I should like to express my appreciation. I think the hon. member is a credit to his constituency and to his father who preceded him.
I should also like to remark on the opening speech of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Hare). He is a man with considerable experience in business and trade in the west. He, too, has brought out some of the problems people there are facing. I think he is going to make a contribution to the factual input that has to go into the policies of any government. I think the country is being well served by the calibre of members who have come to this House in the last few years.
Recently, a very able and experienced man by the name of William Simon, who was secretary treasurer of the United States under President Nixon and President Ford, wrote a book called "It is Time to Tell the Truth". I should like to recommend it to everyone in Canada. It is a terrible indictment of politicians, civil servants, bankers, newspapers, the electronic media-he names names and is careful to name each one who is honest and who speaks up for the truth, just as he names those who do not. I recommend the book to all Canadians. What he describes in his own country, the United States, applies with devastating truth to the current situation in Canada.
There are people in this country who are trying to tell the truth; there are many more in high places who are not. Some of these people are genuinely, sincerely ignorant. Some are unable to remove themselves from the partisanship of their party. Some are smart and know what is happening, but are frightened to express different views from the current mythology of their profession. To me, these people are no longer intellectuals but are part of a brown-nosed pyramid seeking to ooze their way up in this pyramid, to win places of power and prestige. My parliamentary word for this latter group is "nit-wits".
Last week one more instance of this sad sickness that has such a hold on some of our senior civil servants, was demonstrated. On Friday, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) delivered his budget speech. I should like to quote from page 13 of that prepared speech as follows:
I have also concluded that it is essential to amend the Income Tax Act to change the treatment of income debentures and term preferred shares.
That means nothing to 99.9 per cent of us. What a mess it is. The quotation continues:
These securities are currently treated as equities for tax purposes, even though they are essentially debt obligations. As a result, income earned on such securities by banks and other financial institutions is tax-exempt. For the most part they are used for the financing of a relatively small number of multinational
The Budget-Mr. A. Hamilton
and large Canadian corporations. Their use has resulted in a very substantial loss of revenues to the federal and provincial governments. This has been of concern not just to me but also to my provincial colleagues.
When you think that statement through, Mr. Speaker, and realize the significance of what lies under it, you find that, in plain terms, there was an inequitable tax loophole for large corporations that the government was plugging.
The minister tells us that the government has had this under consideration for some period of time, yet, during that time a deputy minister sat on a board of directors of a large commercial company while it was arranging a massive rip-off of the public treasury. His responsibility was to sit on the board of that company and protect the public interest, yet all he did was report to the government that this scheme was being hatched and helped the minister get it approved by the government before the budget was introduced.
They even went further and put words into the minister's mouth to make absolutely sure that the new budget would not apply to this company now in the top big ten of the oil industry in Canada.
And again at page 13 of the minister's budget speech he said:
The proposed amendments will generally apply to any such securities issued after tonight. They will not apply to issues outstanding or committed. Nor will they affect the tax treatment of common and ordinary preferred shares.
What reads as an innocent statement in the budget is the amount of truth which the government is giving to the people of Canada on how long it took them to plug this rip-off of the public treasury and the taxpayers. At the same time that it was planning to stop this loophole, representatives sat down with members of a commercial company, including a high-placed official from the board of directors, and planned to hold the budget up until this plan went through. How can one find a parliamentary word to describe that type of game?
It could have been retroactive.

The minister made it quite clear that his decision regarding budget matters was finalized on Saturday morning. There are many commercial transactions going on all over the country-

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the parliamentary secretary interfered because he ties himself up with this horrible thing that has happened, this immorality. The minister is an honest man, and in this whole thing he appears as a cuckold. If you do not understand that word, look it up in the dictionary. It is parliamentary. The deputy minister was exposed by his minister as being one or more of the following: (a) incompetent; (b) disloyal to the principles of the government; or (c) carrying improper orders from the government. Which one of those things he is I do not know, but that is enough. Neither the minister nor his parliamentary secretary should insult this

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. A. Hamilton
country by saying they are protecting the secrecy of the budget. Any competent civil servant knows how to delay matters if the government does not want something done when it is against the public interest. If that civil servant is protecting the public interest, he could suggest all sorts of devices, such as committee meetings, or other delays until after the budget is over.
It is time to tell the truth, Mr. Speaker. The government knew that this tax loophole was there and it was not in the public interest. It was planning to plug the loophole, and yet at the same time it was planning and working to perpetrate a scheme on hard-pressed taxpayers. It ordered that the shareholders of Pacific Petroleums be paid off at $20 a share above market price. Heaven knows that the PC party has tried for years to have Canadians own the majority of shares in all Canadian companies.
We have our policies ready, but never, never did we plan to ask Canadians to pay more than the market price of any shares. We appreciated foreign investment when we needed it. But as Conservatives, we did not like foreign investors so much that we would ask Canadians to pay 50 per cent more for shares than they are worth. Phillips Petroleum, the U.S.A. company, must be laughing all the way to the bank on this one.
This type of immorality makes it difficult to show any form of charity to this government. The Minister of Finance knows that over the years some of us-and I include myself-have tried very hard to do the same thing as the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont did, and that is to give him evidence that there are other sources of authority besides these nit-wits who advise the Minister of Finance to do these horrible things to our country and to the people of this land. As the minister knows, when we debated Bill C-7 about a month ago, I put on the record for the umpteenth time that we were suffering not from a demand-pull type of inflation which is sending the prices up, but from cost-push inflation. I listed the causes, as I have done many times in the House. First is the cost of government, second, the increase of the money supply. If one charts the increase it will be found that it corresponds exactly with rising prices. Third, are the interest rates. I can recall when 31k per cent and 4 per cent was looked on as high interest rate by the government. The bank rate has now risen from 7 per cent to 10.75 per cent in the last few months. Land costs around our cities are forcing up prices so that the worker has to ask for more and more money just to buy a home.
Labour-management confrontation is a tremendous cost to the country. We borrow obsolete techniques to work out difficulties between labour and management. Everybody suffers, particularly the consumer. Another example which I gave in my speech a month ago is the lack of fundamental knowledge which advisers to the government have of how to utilize this great opportunity which the financial system of the world gives to Canada at this hour, namely, the fluctuating value of the dollar. It is our system of helping a country that has gone down, for whatever reason, to get up and get going again. Instead of letting this force work, we have these nitwits in Washington and Ottawa advising their respective governments

to put up interest rates, and, in the case of Canada, to borrow abroad and join a gambling game on the value of our exchange.
I was looking at an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail the other day. This paper used to represent the business section of Canada. The headline reads "Chretien's paranoia".
I do not know whether or not that term is parliamentary. This is the minister's paranoia with regard to the exchange rate. It is not Chretien's paranoia. A lawyer from Shawinigan does not pay much attention to the exchange rate. He has been taken in by these people who look at the exchange rate as simply something that is causing bad headlines, not realizing that the exchange rate is the way the system works to help any country out of its trouble.
It means to our exporters of basic materials and finished materials that they should get out into the market and balance the international balance for us. This is the elementary truth. This country is not weak, it is strong, %ut for a group of nit-wits putting on the brakes every time the country tries to get out of its trouble, and we were coming out of our trouble these last six months.
The government did not listen to the Economic Council of Canada and all its recommendations over the last five years to move away from the type of budgeting it was following to potential budgeting. The country was still trying to get up and get going. For five years we have been at a stagnation level.
The floating dollar is the best system, under the present world financial system, to help countries like Canada out of their trouble. Instead, we are borrowing money, undertaking obligations abroad, and raising the interest rates because the Americans are raising interest rates. This is bad. First, it interferes with the forces at work that would save us. Second, it is a beautiful chance for the speculators to make money hand over fist out of the Canadian people.
Years ago we thought that an exchange fund would help us stabilize our money and help us get over these dips in our economy. However, that was when dips in the economy were only there for a few months. Now the dips have been there for four or five years.
When you have been gambling on your own exchange, you are not gambling with a few guys buying and selling your dollars. You are gambling against all the Euro dollars of the world, all the money that the multinationals have floating around looking for quick profits. You are gambling against the $100 billion to $200 billion in petro dollars. There is no way we can compete with that. We should have learned that 15 or 18 years ago when we were clobbered in 1962 with just a small sum of Euro dollars.
It is horrible to sit and watch a country make the same mistake twice, but it is the same nit-wits giving advice now as then. I wish to give hon. members some idea in figures of how large is this liability in our world trade, including tangible and intangible items. It is over $100 billion a year. In most
November 21, 1978

business transactions, the terms are for 30, 60, 90, 180 and sometimes 210 days.
The biggest racket in the world today is to live and profit on the other person's nickel. Translated into business terms, that means delaying making your payments for as long as possible and hoping the other guy will pay his debts to you as quickly as possible. Vice versa, if we pay as quickly as possible, and our debtors take as long as possible to repay us, there is a long period of liability. I wish to show how big that is.
If our total trade is $100 billion and our trade deals are on a 30-day basis, in mathematical terms you have a $10 billion liability at any given moment of buying and selling dollars. Suppose the average length of time for a transaction settlement were 90 days, the hypothetical liability would be roughly one quarter, or $25 billion. More and more people are going for 180 days. Arithmetically, the liability then is $50 billion.
Even a little country like Canada, with its trade figure of around $100 billion a year, using a hypothetical example, cannot begin, with a $5 billion or $10 billion reserve fund, to cope with these tremendous demands that might occur if you take the widest extremes in the terms of trade.
This is known to Germany. They had their currency raided, as did France and Italy. The United Kingdom had its currency raided over and over again. The United States could not stand up. Why should Canada try to get into this type of racket? Other nations have experienced the reality.
I am not going to be entirely negative. I can recommend certain corrective actions. First, all these nations are aware of our trouble. The conference at Bonn illustrated that. Why not do the practical thing and establish bilateral defensive agreements with each one of our trading partners roughly equivalent to our potential liability in trade between our two countries? If you did that with your four or five main trading partners, you would not have to worry too much if there were a shortage one way or another in the daily demand on the respective currencies.
The second proposal regards export taxes. If you do a study of the export taxes applied to Japanese, European, Canadian, American and other goods, you will find that our exports are carrying a bigger load of tax on their back going into the markets than do those of our competitors, such as Germany, for example. I suggest that we as a government should guarantee unilaterally to our exporters that our tax load on them will be no greater than the Japanese exporter has to bear, that they will at least compete equally, and thus we will destroy this temporary great imbalance in trade in our respective countries.
Third, we should keep our domestic costs down, which is similar to saying you are for motherhood.
Fourth, there should be new types of trade institutions. It is 14 years since I stood up on this side of the House and proposed a list of six different types of new trade institutions to grapple with the problem that I foresaw with the coming great increase in world trade. It would be worthwhile for serious young members of this House to read that speech made in October, 1964.
The Budget-Mr. A. Hamilton
Fifth, Canada, above all nations, should be pushing very hard for an international unit of exchange. There used to be a member in this parliament years ago, now deceased, who belonged to the New Democratic Party. He was the first person I ever heard talk about this in this House. He was talking about it 20 years ago, and he was right.
Since that time we have had the special drawing rights which are a step forward. However, until all the nations of the world accept the fact that they have to put all their business into one house, have a unit of exchange which is worldwide, get rid of the dollar exchange, sterling exchange, and other national currencies, we will be in trouble. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned for the recess I was putting before the House a number of corrective measures which could be used in substitution for these costly and, I am afraid, fatal techniques of borrowing abroad and using the interest rate as a method of protecting our dollar.
I listed the bilateral defence arrangements between our natural trading partners and I put down as number two on my list the equality of taxes on Canadian exports as opposed to those of our trading partners. The third was the need to keep down domestic costs-and the fourth was the new type of trade institutions, which was very important and which deserves a speech by itself. Fifth, I was just starting to talk about the special drawing rights or international unit of exchange. This is not a new idea, as all the quantitative analysis of the major 20 industrial countries in the last 20 years indicates. There is no currency available to the trading nations sufficient to carry the weight of all this huge world trade, and Canada in particular and all the other trading nations in general should join together to push for an international unit of exchange in the next two or three years.
The sixth corrective action could be taken if we faced up to reality and told the people of the world the truth-that all the high hopes we had during the Geneva agreement on tariffs and trade, using the obsolete tariff techniques, have ended in failure. We have developed into a rich man's club, handing out a few crumbs to the poor countries standing at the gate. Without going into that any further at this time, I would like to say I have tried on several occasions over the last 14 years to put forward a constructive theory which I call growth rate exchange. It has been used in several instances. It was used in the steel community in Europe. It was used in the automobile

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. A. Hamilton
agreement here between Canada and the United States. I think this is the technique which we should be employing in product after product so that there is real equality in bargaining power between the nations with certain resources they are trading off by growth rate exchanges.
The final point I wish to make in the last minutes remaining to me concerns interest rates. The government is paranoid on this score, believing firmly that it must protect the dollar by using the device of raising interest rates since this will be better for the country than letting the dollar float freely. They are frightened because if the dollar goes down one point-one cent-cost of living in Canada will go up one-tenth of a point. So it takes a change of ten cents in the international value of our dollar before our cost of living goes up 1 per cent. But if you look at the comparative cost with which interest burdens this country, you realize once again, under this correlative analysis approach to all capital intensive enterprises, be it buying a home or a farm or building a $2 billion enterprise, that 75 per cent of the cost at present interest rates is made up of interest charges and that if you increase those interest costs by 50 per cent, as we have done in the last eight months, you add on to the cost of producing goods in Canada much more than you add on to the cost of goods bought by consumers through a drop in the international value of our dollar. The proportions are immense and amount to many billions of dollars over the cost to this nation in a one-year period.
I cannot develop this theme at great length at this time but I am simply saying, as bluntly and as candidly as I can, that to move along the road of raising interest rates as a device to keep our dollar from dropping is going to be costly for the people of Canada over the next year or so. And please God we can get out of this suicidal mania we have for using this technique which does so much harm to the people of this country, not only with respect to their cost of living but also to their ability to compete with trade rivals all over the world.
Interest costs are going to be much greater than the cost of letting the dollar float freely. The advantages of letting the dollar float freely are that you get rid of speculators because they speculate one against the other-they do not speculate very much, they stabilize the dollar for you-and you do not interfere with the great forces which exist in a free society of correlations, helping a nation that has a currency which is below the usual level to get on its feet again. I cannot emphasize that point too much.
In conclusion, I have tried here to put forward, on top of my criticism of the government and its advisers, my view that the use of the road of interest rates and borrowing abroad is going to be very hard on our economy over the next few months.
I predict that if we get these interest rates off our back within the next year, the dollar will come to about 90 cents through the very efforts being made by our producers to sell abroad and to produce goods at home. I predict that industries such as forestry, mining and the valued added industries, will all

join in that growth. This is the way the minister could balance his budget and get rid of the deficits.
For five years now we have been in this stagnation-

I had just completed my last sentence, but I would like to repeat it loud and clear. I would predict that if we prevent interest rates from rising for another six or eight months, the economy will stage a recovery, after five years of stagnation, and that by the end of this coming year our currency will achieve an international value of 90 cents. I believe that this is about the best level for our dollar for the best operation of our system at the present time. There would be more people working, more tax revenues coming into the coffers of the government, and it would alleviate our deficits abroad and at home.
This type of proposal is not without some merit or rational support in the economic analysis which I have given in my speech. I know that it is too late now for the government to change this budget, but I do hope that in the budget they must now be preparing for next spring, the government will not push our economy too hard and will give us a chance to live and to let this country do the job for which it is well prepared and which it is willing to do.
Hear, hear!

My first remark tonight, Mr. Speaker, is one of congratulation to my colleague, the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston). I thought that his speech yesterday in the budget debate was not only one of the best speeches by a new member, but certainly one of the better speeches I have heard in this House. He is a welcome addition to this place.
I would like to indicate now my support for the budget, for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the government's fiscal policy. It is an extremely responsible budget and one that will be beneficial to the economy over the medium and long term. I am one of those who are of the opinion that what is required at the present time is confidence in the economy and the business sector. I believe that this relates to the stability of the dollar, which I am pleased to see has occurred to some extent in recent days.
I do not think that the dollar would be in its present state of stability if the Minister of Finance had adopted some of the suggestions put forth by the opposite side for large spending programs resulting in a large increase to the deficit, which would have made the problem to which the previous speaker referred much worse.
The budget was consistent with what has been a relatively long period of government fiscal policy in this direction, which
November 21, 1978

started with the Macdonald budget in March, 1977, through three budgets brought down by the present Minister of Finance. It is consistent with the initiatives taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on August 1, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Abbott), research and development under the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) and the consensus drawn from the premiers across Canada. I would also like to mention in that regard the very excellent work done by the member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) in putting together many of the initiatives which have found their way into government policy.
I would like to contrast that consistent approach to Fiscal responsibility with some of the comments we have heard from the opposite side since this debate began. I read the press, and have been in the places across this country where members from the official opposition have been speaking on the banquet circuit. They have been making comments which are really quite detrimental in terms of the kinds of cuts they would advocate. They have been talking about slashing the public service on the one hand, and on the other they come into this House and plead almost daily for more spending and that none of these programs be cut. Indeed, this afternoon, in a committee of this House which I attended, I believe all of the speakers from the opposite side wanted the ministry involved to restore all of the cuts which have taken place. I cannot understand how they can argue for significant cuts, and then as soon as they are applied, join hands and argue it should not happen.
I would like to contest some of the comments made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). I do not think that he intended to mislead the House, but I believe he did take some liberty in some of the viewpoints he put forward. By carefully edging around some hard facts and accusations, he may have left impressions which I think should not stand on the record. He indicated there may have been some patronage associated with the farming out to the private sector of research, and that this government may have destroyed the initiatives taken by the Diefenbaker government in research and development. He also took insupportable positions in terms of the growth of the Prime Minister's office and the Privy Council office. I would like to draw hon. members' attention to some of the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition as reported in yesterday's Hansard at page 1287. He is talking there about patronage in terms of farming work out rather than doing the job within the public service. It reads:
First of all, there has been a very insignificant cut, certainly not as significant as is possible, in the practice of contracting out. This is a very dangerous practice, dangerous to our system of government because it allows a government that wants to, to get around the protection against patronage, to get around the protection against incompetence that is built into the Public Service Commission-
Further on he says:
It is also very, very clear that there has been an immense capacity for abuse not only of spending but of controls to ensure that there is protection against patronage. That capacity was there, and I suggest that if this was a government
The Budget-Mr. Milne
that was very seriously concerned about practising restraint we would have had some significant cuts in the practice of contracting out.
If the Leader of the Opposition is alleging that there is patronage associated with the contracting out policies of the government, then he should be very specific and bring forward instances, rather than make comments such as that. Just prior to making that comment, Hansard reports him as saying:
-proposals such as the phasing out of forestry stations, the phasing out of weather ships on the west coast, the phasing out of weather forecasting which could have meant a matter of life and death in the province of my colleague from St. John's.
The Leader of the Opposition complains about lack of restraint, and when the government restraint program does wash across some of these other areas which have been handed over to the private sector, he raises a similar type of complaint. I am surprised that he would take such a strong stand against the private sector.
He made another comment yesterday, and it may be that he did not consult the public accounts for the past year or, the supplementary estimates for 1978-79. I am referring to the ludicrous charge he made that spending on the Privy Council office increased by 86 per cent in the first six months of this year over the first six months of last year. He also stubbornly maintained that the Privy Council office and the Prime Minister's office had hired respectively 80 and 54 new people last year. When this baseless accusation was first made in this House a couple of weeks ago by, I believe, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), the Leader of the Opposition must have either been away, not listening, or maybe both, because at that time it was explained that budgets and expenditures are compared on a yearly basis, not just a half yearly basis. That was brought to the attention of the House in the response of the Prime Minister to the question raised by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). According to the public accounts for last year, the total expenditures for the Privy Council office, if services provided by other departments are included, amounted to approximately $26.5 million. According to the blue book of Estimates and Supplementary Estimates A, the comparable figure for this year would be approximately $28 million. That is an increase just under 6 per cent, not 86 per cent. How on earth can a person who is asking the country for confidence in him come up with 86 per cent rather than the correct figure of 6 per cent?
Perhaps I can shed some light on this matter. The cost of various bodies not in any way part of the Privy Council office are charged to the budget of PCO. These bodies include the Canadian Inter-Governmental Secretariat, the Chief Electoral Officer, the Commissioner of Official Languages, the Economic Council of Canada, and the Public Service Staff Relations Board. Surely there is no lack of understanding, on this point, for when he compared the figures for the first six months of this year to those for the first six months of last year, the hon. member for York-Simcoe indicated that he referred strictly to the day to day operating expenses of the Privy Council. A comparison of these figures-not forgetting that such compari-

on a comparative basis, we had about 146 people in Canada working in 1977 for every 100 working in 1965. That compares with 130 in Australia and 128 in the United States. However, in most other industrialized countries the size of the work force has changed very little. In fact, as I said a minute ago, in the case of West Germany, the size of the work force in 1977 was actually smaller than it was in 1965. I think we should be fairly optimistic in those terms.
I do not want to deal entirely in statistics, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to refer the House and people interested in the economy to the Toronto Star of Monday, November 20, specifically to an article in the financial section headlined "Money and markets". It contains the comment that considerably more growth in the economy is expected in 1979. Let me summarize what the author of that article indicates. Jobs in Canada will increase by at least 4 per cent, which I think is low; I feel our growth rate will be more in line with the prediction of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). That article predicts on a comparable basis that growth in the United Kingdom will be about 3.3 per cent; in the United States, 3.6 per cent; in France, 2.7 per cent; and in West Germany, 3.5 per cent. Again, when you look at those countries you will see they make up the majority of the stronger industrialized countries, yet none of them will have growth that will compare with Canada's, if these figures are accurate.
The other point I want to put on the record as strongly as I can is my support for some of the structural items in this budget. It seems to me the budget supports, as have previous budgets, efforts to become more self-sufficient in food and, more important, to become even more self-sufficient in energy, and to support and advance the position of the manufacturing sector which, if one looks at the creation of jobs, is without question the greatest creator of jobs whenever there is expansion.
It seems to me what we have is a country blessed with a tremendous number of resources. We have probably the most highly educated work force in the world. We have support policies that have come in through this government in the past two or three years, particularly in terms of support for small business and a better tax position for business in general. In fact, the president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business now suggests that perhaps business in this country, particularly small business, has as good or a better tax position than any other country.
We have a research and development policy which I do not think many other countries can equal. Our labour rates, thanks to the kind of policy that has been followed in the past three years by this government, would indicate now that the increase in labour costs is growing much more slowly than in the United States. We have a dollar which gives us a real advantage in terms of exports.
I commend the Minister of Industry, T rade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) for giving leadership in his sectoral reports. If people have not read the consensus of those reports, I suggest it is worth their while to do so, because it really indicates for the first time that there has been a very substantive meeting of
The Budget-Mr. Milne
minds between business leaders in this country and some of the leaders of the larger unions. It is significant in this regard that when they came and sat around the table, after some initial difficulty, the business people were not asking for more support, more subsidies and higher tariffs, and labour was not asking for raises that would endanger the well-being of employers. They were looking at where the strengths of this country are and how they could best maximize them.
In terms of the energy situation, I think I should refer back to Mr. Macdonald's budget of two years ago in May by which resource exploration was allowed as a 100 per cent cost write-off. This was the beginning of a pretty important policy which has resulted in a fairly significant increase in the inventory of energy we have available to us today.
I am anxiously awaiting, as I am sure other hon. members are, the National Energy Board report, because I think it will probably show that we have improved remarkably our inventory position of natural gas and oil.
I would think the measure in this budget to allow a better tax benefit for mining development costs will have a very important effect on the tar sands. I take it, from what I have been able to understand, that this measure will apply to the tar sands. The tar sands will be defined as a mining operation, and I certainly think it should be.
As a matter of fact, the materials handling aspect of the Syncrude plant will move more material in one year than all other mines in Canada put together. This is an enormous mining operation. What we need is a good deal more development in the tar sands. Surely with this type of incentive, the private sector will be encouraged even more to participate.
It would seem that if we are to meet the kind of energy needs that we will face in this country in the future, we should be hearing the announcement of the start of a new tar sands plant every three years. When you consider that they require in the neighbourhood of a $3 billion or $4 billion investment, you will see that this will certainly require the assembling of a good deal of technology, training of manpower and money. This will be important, as indeed it will be in terms of developing new uranium mines. I think the location of them has been identified in many cases, and it will also be important in terms of having a better and more healthy coal mining operation.
With our energy needs of the future, surely oil from the heavy oil deposits, oil from the tar sands, uranium and coal from mines will be the basis on which our energy equation will operate, to a large degree.
This measure which has been granted the mining industry, as applied to the development of energy, will be one of the important incentives. I hope it is and I hope that other countries will follow the resource policy of this government. I do not suppose it is for me, standing where I am, to suggest that to other countries, but it seems to me that, in terms of the dollar, one of the difficulties in the United States results from the amount of energy they are purchasing from outside the country. That has had a somewhat weakening effect on that

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Milne
economy, and that, in turn, has not done anything to strengthen the Canadian dollar.
I congratulate this government for having the kind of policies it has had for the development of energy resources. Had we not had these policies over the past two or three years, when the tax system really responded to the needs of the industry to improve the inventory, this country would be faced with the necessity of purchasing a much larger proportion of its energy, and that would have a very weakening effect on the future prospects of our economy.
That is why I am so astounded by the position taken by the opposition, particularly the Leader of the Opposition, in response to the government's initiative in terms of Petro-Canada. Having listened to the Leader of the Opposition pontificate his viewpoint in this regard, I must observe that I have not seen very many of his supporters from Atlantic Canada or, indeed, from some areas in Ontario, applaud his approach. It seems to me that most of the applause for his position has come from one part of the country. I have been watching for some members from Atlantic Canada to get up and tell this House they feel as strongly that the Conservative party is right in condemning the government for acquiring a handle on the energy business through Petro-Canada.
It seems to me there are two or three things required in this country in respect of energy policy: One is to have a pricing structure, and another is to have a taxation structure. In addition to that, surely we need some kind of mechanism that sets a time frame within which these projects must be commenced, so that in terms of manpower, money and demand this will be synchronized.
Sometimes this will happen through the private sector and sometimes it will not. Sometimes some of these projects, which will be very important to future needs, will falter as, indeed, the Syncrude plan was in danger of doing. It just seems to me that there are so many reasons why the establishment and perpetuation of Petro-Canada, and the expansion which has taken place in the last two weeks, is a correct government decision that I have real difficulty in understanding the viewpoint of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark).
In the years I have served in this House during this term I have associated myself fairly closely with the energy question.
I have participated on the standing committee in a fairly major way in terms of looking at energy policy in Canada, and I think that if the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition are to be directed at anyone, surely they should be directed at the premier of Alberta. The Alberta Energy Corporation would not have been able to involve itself in many energy projects without the involvement and encouragement of that government. Therefore, it seems to me that when they make these disparaging remarks about their friends who sit on their left over there, they should really be directing such comments to their own province of Alberta.
The objective of Petro-Canada, of course, is different; it is to get involved in the kinds of things it would be difficult for the
[Mr. Milne.)
private sector to do. Perhaps I should not say difficult to do, but things that the private sector might not voluntarily do. I refer to continually putting millions and millions of dollars into exploration in the high Arctic islands, realizing that delivery of natural gas and oil, if they should find it, may be some years away. As a matter of fact, millions of dollars have been put into the Beaufort Sea and Mackenzie Delta, where delivery even of that resource, along with the resource of the tar sands and heavy oil, is still some time away. We certainly need this kind of corporation for that.
I am also waiting in the House to hear the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) applaud when the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for York-Simcoe say derogatory things about Petro-Canada. I understand from something which came across my desk the other day that the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton is one of the directors of the Committee for an Independent Canada. I would like to know how he really feels when his leader who sits in front of him stands up and welcomes the multinational companies' operations in Canada as a good thing. You can almost hear them applauding down the street, him being a director of that organization and his leader being completely opposed to the Petro-Canada acquisition. It certainly seems odd to me.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are about to rise and I just want to conclude by saying that I wish I had time to talk about research and development. Since I do not have time, I will leave it to other speakers, but I categorically deny the statement the Leader of the Opposition made yesterday when he indicated-
