Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Peel-Duff-erin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne) who just preceded me. He made reference to the sectoral task force reports which have been published by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. He recommended that all hon. members take the time to read these reports. Perhaps he would be well advised to instruct some of the members of his own cabinet to read the reports, because if they had, perhaps they would have developed a different stance with respect to some of the policy initiatives which were outlined in the budget. I refer specifically to the report by the sectoral task force of the Canadian tourist industry, wherein it states at page 28 that the airport user-pay policy makes air transportation in Canada non-competitive with that of the United States and is detrimental to Canadian tourism development. That statement was made before the increase in the air transportation tax levied as a result of the minister's budget last Thursday. If the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has not read that report, perhaps he should; and if he has read it, perhaps he should pay some attention to the contents of the report.
In his opening remarks in introducing his budget last Thursday, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) stressed that it is important in this country that we create a climate-or an
November 21, 1978

atmosphere, I believe was his exact word-of stability and certainty. He also pointed out that that was a common theme which was advanced to him as he travelled throughout the country discussing the budget with various leaders in industry, with economists, provincial politicians and members of labour.
He also indicated that they felt very strongly about the fact that we must take initiatives at this time to restore some semblance of confidence and stability. That desire has been prevalent for quite a number of years. It has been known for some time that there has been a pressing desire to restore our economic climate to some state of confidence and stability. While we recognize that that is a laudable requirement, it must nevertheless not be overlooked that this confidence crisis which we seem to be facing has been caused in almost every respect by the mismanagement of this government.
The Minister of Finance in his speech also tried to lead us into believing that at long last he has mapped a course on behalf of this government which will lead us out of the economic doldrums. He stated very bravely, as reported at page 1205 of Hansard:
So tonight I have brought down a budget to build further confidence and to ensure continued competitiveness.
Those are indeed laudable objectives, objectives which I think every member of the House would support. But we have to ask ourselves whether or not these objectives are achievable by this government. Personally I doubt it, because it does not seem to be the nature of this government to be able to grapple with the things that need to be done. At the present time they are too preoccupied with an election and are addressing their priorities toward improving their electoral fortunes.
Implicit in the budget as well was a call once again to all Canadians to respond, to rally as good citizens behind the government. There is some difficulty there, Mr. Speaker, because Canadians are being asked to rally and respond to a government which is worn out, which is beleaguered and which is tired. While this kind of rally is probably necessary in the national interest, I submit it will not be forthcoming under the present circumstances because Canadians have been stung all too often by this government and simply do not have any confidence in this group. For this government, sir, has lingered on far too long. It is on borrowed time. It is stale. It is beleaguered, as I said earlier, and it has developed a kind of fortress mentality geared to survival at any cost. In the process, Canadians of every walk of life have lost their confidence and their trust in this administration. Very simply put, Canadians do not believe this government any longer and they do not trust it. That is the number one issue in this country today.
And why should they, sir? Let me review their record briefly. It was this government that said in 1974 that it would not impose wage and price controls. It did in 1975. This is the same group that promised to reduce inflation to 4 per cent by 1978. It is 1978 now, and inflation is at 9 per cent. It was this same government whose leader in 1975 all but abandoned the free market economy declaring that in the future, government would intervene more, that government would be more
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski
authoritative. It is interesting to read some of the statements uttered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at that time. An article in the Ottawa Citizen of January 20, 1976, notes some of them. On the issue of big government he said:
'The state is important, the government is important. It means there's going to be not less authority in our lives, but perhaps more.'
The same article, referring to big business and big labour, quotes him again:
-the government is going to take a larger role in running institutions, as we're doing now with our anti-inflation controls, but as we'll presumably be doing even after the controls are ended-'
That was also on December 28. In fact, a great deal of uncertainty and instability was created in the Canadian economic climate.
In his television address on August 1, 1978, we see a complete flip-flop when the Prime Minister said:
We will remove the intrusions of many government policies and regulations from individuals and businesses; in some cases this will mean returning functions to the private sector, in others it will mean removing the heavy hand of government and its drag on personal initiatives.
We saw that elaborated a bit more in the Speech from the Throne when two objectives were outlined. One was to impose severe restraints on government spending and the other was to encourage vigorous expansion of the private sector. Canadians are asking themselves how these two opposite positions can be balanced. What philosophical shade of the Prime Minister are we to believe?
While this new initiative toward the private sector is being advanced, this government sanctions and, in fact, encourages the biggest coup ever staged in this country-the takeover of Pacific 66 by Petro-Canada. They have joined the big boys in the oil patch, committing the Canadian economy to an expenditure of $1.4 billion. That is a huge financial drag on the economy of Canada. There is also the purchase of Nordair for $28 million. Of course, we are going to turn that over to the private sector within a year. We all remember the commitment made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) when the takeover of de Havilland and Canada Air were initiated in 1974, and he said it was not the view of the government that de Havilland by itself or Canada Air should be operated as a Crown corporation. That was in 1974; the company is still intact.
We have just witnessed an unprecedented government intrusion in the private sector on the most massive scale ever witnessed in this country. There is no question about that.
This is the same government that made an oil pricing agreement with the province of Alberta and before the ink was dry, tried to break the agreement.
This is the same government that, in its commitment to the private sector, has unilaterally set out to withdraw the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act. That is clearly a very regressive measure. In response to that action, the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce wrote to the Prime Minister on October 4, 1978, as follows:

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski
The Edmonton Chamber of Commerce views the repeal of this act as retrogressive and such repeal would place the private sector of the utilities, electrical and natural gas industries in an unequal position with the tax free municipal and provincially owned utilities.
Later in the same letter they wrote:
This is another illustration of the lack of permanence and stability so vital for a viable and effective private sector.
Who has created the uncertainty, Mr. Speaker? Who has created the instability? Who has undermined confidence in this country? These are the very actions that serve this purpose.
This is the same government that promised in 1974 to revamp the grain handling system from the granary to the ship in the harbour. I am glad the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is here tonight. He used that expression time and time again in the west. Today our system does not have the capability to move to export in excess of 21 million tons of grain, the figure we achieved in 1972-73. The situation in this country today is nothing short of chaotic-a paralysis in the grain handling industry with sales lost, deferred, and the system plugged. In spite of the minister's efforts to "strain the system" as he puts it so glowingly from time to time, we are not able to achieve the level of 21.4 million tons that we achieved in 1972-73.
This is the same government that promised that not one rail line would be abandoned against the wishes of producers. I should like to quote the Minister of Transport in regard to that, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press on June 11, 1974, as follows:
Otto Lang said 'as long as the Liberal party forms the government and as long as producers wish to continue to deliver to the elevator of their choice, not one rail line will be abandoned.'
But what happened, Mr. Speaker? I should invite the Minister of Transport to visit the constituency of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart). He would witness a very sorry scene there. The farmers in that area are hostile and are reacting. I understand they are burning an effigy of the president of the Manitoba pool, they are so unhappy with the decision brought down by the Prairie Rail Action Committee. This is outright hostility toward those hollow promises.
The chairman of the Prairie Rail Action Committee is a professor of economics in Regina. An article in the Manitoba Co-Operator reports as follows:
Anderson said the basic rail network, originally laid out and guaranteed by the federal government to the year 2000, 'is itself an irrational collection of lines derived from a series of politically expedient decisions.'
He said that events show that there is still too much mileage in the basic network and this means continued high rail costs.
If we are to believe the advice the minister is receiving from the chairman of the Prairie Rail Action Committee, we can assume that many more rail lines will be abandoned before this minister and the chairman of the Prairie Rail Action Committee are through in western Canada.
I could go on to talk about inaccuracies with respect ot budgetary deficits and growth targets, the inaccuracy in projections with respect to unemployment, but I think I have said
enough to show there is a very, very marked credibility gap with this government.
Why should Canadians trust the government? The illustrations I have advanced simply mean one thing, they prove that this government does not keep its word. It is a government which has tinkered with the economy, it has tinkered with the books and it has tinkered with parliament. It is a government which shifts from left to right in its policies. It is a government which has lost control. These are the facts and the realities of the situation. I submit that confidence will not be restored by this budget. Confidence in this country can only come from a new government. I know the members opposite are very sensitive. They must be sensitive because we have been pointing out the waste, the extravagance and the mismanagement of this particular group. We are not the only ones. Yes, now there is the press. The press are the bad guys. The press and the opposition are the ones who have caused all the problems. They are the preachers of gloom and doom. And then we come to the provinces. Everybody seems to be against this government. The Toronto Sun says this about the government and the Prime Minister.
The Toronto Sunt

Yes, it is a fairly popular newspaper and its circulation is increasing all the time. Here again the Prime Minister is blaming everybody but himself. The Toronto Sun says this:
Trudeau and his policies have divided, undermined and alienated Canada. Few have started out with the trust and goodwill he had ten years ago; few have misused power and responsibility more crassly. Trudeau has been a one-man wrecking crew-
Trudeau insists he is "the best man" for Canada. Untrue. The record indicates he is the 'worst' man for Canada-and possibly the 'worst' Prime Minister in our history. The sooner Clark gets his job, the sooner Canada will recover.
Hear, hear!
I want to deal with one aspect of the budget which will create and cause a great deal of consternation-
Constipation.
Consternation, sir. Maybe you have never heard of the word before. I know that there are a few afflicted with that other word which you have just used.
Oh, oh!

This has to do with the reduction in the manufacturers' sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent. It concerns a statement made by the Minister of Finance which points out that the Minister of National Revenue will not entertain any applications for refunds of that tax-that is the difference between the 12 per cent and the 9 per cent-in respect of goods on which the 12 per cent tax has been paid.

November 21, 1978

This government is supposed to be the saviour, the friend of the small business community. There is certainly a lack of common sense and a blatant disregard for the small business community in the application and the manner in which that tax will be administered. I can assure you of that, sir. The minister is asking that all those involved ensure that this saving is passed on to the consumer, yet at the same time he is asking the retail dealers in this country to absorb that 3 per cent. I have to say this in all sincerity and I make it in the form of a representation. I ask the Minister of Finance and this government to reconsider that position because it will represent a huge loss on the larger commodities in the hands of the small private entrepreneurs. I have had a number of phone calls today in this regard, and I suspect there will be many more.
I have a wire in my hand which I will put on the record. I think it summarizes a view that is probably widely held in this country. This telegram comes from the general manager and principal dealer of Parkland Chrysler Ltd. in Lloydminster, Alberta. It states as follows:
Regarding the federal budget announcement of the reduction in federal sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent on Thursday, November 16 we join with FADA-
FADA means the Federation of the Automobile Dealers Association. The telegram goes on to say:
-in protesting the lack of rebate to dealers. This decision alone will cost our small dealership approximately $18,000.
I implore the minister to reconsider his decision, which would be only just and fair, and to entertain applications for refund of that 3 per cent tax differential. It will serve as a very serious blow and hardship on many small dealers.
We have talked about the importance of stability and certainty. We have talked about the necessity of having a coordinated approach to the administration of federal government programs. I want to deal now with the application of the new airport tax. I believe this is a clear, classic example where we have an unco-ordinated, disjointed approach by the federal government in its attempts to pursue an objective, and the objective is to improve Canada's tourist industry. This particular measure imposes a disproportionate burden upon the regional and third level air carriers. The percentage, in terms of the application of this tax, will be roughly in the area of 3 per cent on a transcontinental flight, while it will be 15 per cent on a small third level or regional flight. I think it is grossly unfair and simply flies in the face of the recommendations that have been advanced by the task force on tourism.
The air transport association of Canada has clearly outlined its position which, I believe, puts the whole question in perspective. I quote from a message by the Air Transport Association which was sent to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) from the president and chief executive officer of the Air Transport Association of Canada.
We believe the extension of the air transportation tax to be contrary to the thrust of other budget measures aimed at providing tax relief and encouraging industrial effort. Not only is the increased tax contrary to the general thrust of your
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski
budget, it is also contrary to the strong recommendations of the government's own task force on tourism which advocated tax relief in the interest of lower prices in transportation and tourism. The increase in the air transportation tax will add to the difficulty of Canadian carriers to compete with American carriers, and could lead to some diversion of travel to departure points located in the U.S.A. We see no evidence of real effort to reduce Transport Canada expenditures and regret that your efforts to reduce government spending did not find $72 million there.
We also view with concern the announced intention to convert the air transportation tax at a later date to a user charge as this will remove it from public view and the close scrutiny of parliament and allow the imposition of charges involving large arbitrary sums at the discretion of the Minister of Transport and his officials which is questionable in principle.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: That said it all.

As my hon. colleague, has suggested, it said it all.
There are a number of other matters on which I would like to have touched. I wanted to develop the matter of the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act. I wanted to talk about the uncertainty that is created by the enlargement of the bureaucratic web, which has created uncertainty, confusion, and downright hostility in many areas. However, time does not permit.
I do want to conclude by saying a few words about the grain industry and our inability to pursue the market potential that is available to us, and the impact that it does have upon our economy. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) pointed out very capably last Friday that there are many areas where we have missed golden opportunities as a resut of the misguided priorities of this government. One is in the field of pursuing our potential in the world grain export market.
On the prairies today there is frustration, hardship and downright anger as a result of our inability to deliver. We are losing sales every day. This is hurting Canada's reputation. We are losing our prominence as a renowned supplier of grain on the export market. It is costing each and every Canadian a lot of money.
If we look at the grains industry in terms of what it means to the Canadian economy, we find that traditionally our grain exports have been in the order of $2.5 billion. They constitute in excess of 60 per cent of our total agricultural exports. Hence, this is a major contributor to Canada's trade picture, particularly with regard to our balance of payments.
Directly related to the $2.5 billion of world exports we make annually, for every $1 of grain that is exported, $2 is generated directly through expenditures on inputs such as machinery, fertilizer, fuel, oil and the various input supplies that go to produce that product. When that $2 filters through the economy, it creates an induced multiplier impact of $5.5. That creates jobs, builds plants, builds homes for factory workers, gives them the capacity to buy cars and improves our technology. It stimulates investment, and we need stimulation at this time, particularly with our plants running at about 85 per cent capacity.

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. McRae
In addition, this original $1 for the sale of export grain ultimately generates $1 to $1.50 worth of revenue to the federal government in the form of taxes. We find that $2.5 billion worth of grain export sales adds $5 billion directly to the farm input sector, it creates $13.75 billion worth of economic activity, and it provides $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion in terms of revenue to the federal government. That is on the positive side.
In this last crop year, we missed opportunities for sales of some four million tons of grain.
Oh, oh!
That is true. If you can prove it is not true, stand up and give me that proof.
You give the proof.

I have the proof. Canadian Wheat Board spokesmen-and I trust them more than I do the hon. member-have indicated that we have lost sales of four million tons of grain. That represents about $500 million which the producers have lost. In addition, the farm input sector has lost $1 billion, and the total economy has lost some $2.75 billion in economic spinoff.
We lost the sale of four million tons of grain last year. So far this year we have been told by the Canadian Wheat Board that 2.3 million tons of grain have been deferred for later delivery. That is worth $350 million. The members of the wheat board say those are potentially lost sales.
We can no longer carry on without a strategic plan to improve our capability and capacity to remove grain. It is disappointing, disturbing and unhealthy to the farm economy. It is unhealthy for the general economy.
I see my time is up. I hope I will have an opportunity at some later date to develop this further.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure listening to my very good friend and respected colleague. I do not think there is anyone on that side more respected by those on this side than the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). However, we do differ on some points from time to time. Before expressing my thoughts,
I would like to deal with a couple of the points he mentioned.
The hon. member referred to the oil price agreement between Alberta and the federal government. That should be considered carefully. In that agreement it is stated that the Canadian price should not go higher than the U.S. price so that we are not put in an unfavourable competitive industrial position with the Americans because of our oil. I would have preferred the government to have priced the oil in the same way as the Americans did, with one price for new oil and another one for old oil. Under those circumstances, the province of Alberta would suffer a good deal more than it does at present.
I would like to deal briefly with Petro-Can. I cannot understand why the opposition is making such a fuss about the
[Mr. Mazankowski.)
acquisition of Pacific Petroleums. Over 95 per cent of our oil resources are foreign-owned and controlled. This is a very dangerous position, particularly in view of the fact that our conventional supply is likely to peter out over the next ten to fifteen years.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member how acquiring Petro-Can has increased the oil supply in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, there are many ways one can do that. I do not intend at this point-
Oh, oh!

All right, I will deal with it briefly. We need to have some holdings which we can develop. There are some heavy oil holdings which may or may not be developed. Protecting that supply is very important. As this industry is almost totally controlled outside our boundaries, it is time we started moving in this direction.
There is a third point that is important. Most Canadians do not believe the industry. There is a lack of credibility about the industry. Therefore, it makes sense for the government of Canada to have a piece of the action and to keep an eye on what is happening. The monitoring factor is relatively important.
I now wish to deal with specific parts of the budget. First, I will deal briefly with the Canadian economy in general and how it relates to the economies of other nations. There is a kind of negative attitude which was mentioned by the hon. member for Vegreville as well as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), although in a somewhat different way, regarding our economy. This attitude is harmful to Canadians. It is harmful to their attitude toward their government and the country. I will give an example.
The borrowing bill has been before the House for about a month, since October 20 I believe. Much has been said about the growth of the national debt. It is said it is growing at a horrendous rate and that we will be bankrupt in a short time. However, no real analysis has been made of the debt.
Debt, whether national or private, is relative to something. If I owe $5,000 today and ten years ago I owed $2,000, who is to say at what time I am better off financially? That would depend on my income, assets, and so on. These are factors which must be taken into consideration. If we look at the growth or lack of growth in our national debt, we must do that in terms of the gross national product. Let us look at this briefly in terms of the GNP. The net national debt in 1952 was
51.7	per cent of the gross national product for that year. The net national debt in 1962, the last full year in which the Conservative party was in power, was 33.4 per cent of the GNP for that year. In 1972, the net national debt was down to 19 per cent of the GNP for that year. In this portion of 1978, the national debt amounts to 18.7 per cent of the GNP. That is a meaningful way of approaching the issue. The debt has not gone up in terms of the gross national product. Indeed, it has
November 21, 1978

declined. The average for the 25-year period from 1952 to the beginning of the present year is 30 per cent. This year, next year and the year after we shall be well below the average for those years I have mentioned.
I am trying to show that the state of the Canadian economy is not nearly as bad as many members on the opposition side would have us believe. There is no doubt that all industrial countries are experiencing great difficulty at the present time. There has been a massive growth in problems of the kind all governments face. We are talking about inflation rates of 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent up to 1950. Now we see inflation rates of at least 5 per cent.
All governments are also facing massive energy problems, coupled with an unprecedented outflow of dollars to purchase or ensure supplies, and the techniques normally used in such circumstances do not work as well as they used to. To show how well Canadians are doing, we must compare ourselves with the other industrial nations with which we trade.
Such as Uganda?

I am going to compare our performance with that of 15 industrial nations outside the Communist world: the United States, West Germany, The Netherlands, Australia, Norway, Belgium, France, Japan, Switzerland, Denmark, United Kingdom, Sweden and Finland. There are a series of indices we could use. It is difficult when you compare these indices at the end, totalling them, but I will deal with that when I get there. The First index I will use has to do with the rise in employment, the number of jobs created. In those 15 countries, in the years 1970-1977-I could take the years between 1974 and 1977 and obtain approximately the same result-Canada was First among the 15, with a 27 per cent growth in the number of jobs. Let us not forget that in the same period there had been a much larger growth in the size of our labour force than was experienced in any of the other countries. For every hundred people in the labour force in 1965, there are 146 today whereas the average for the other six members of the summit group is only nine. I do not have the figures for all those countries in terms of unemployment, but we would certainly be below the average in that respect. On the other hand, our problem is about 500 per cent more acute than those of the other six members of the summit group.
Take another index. The United States department of agriculture carried out a study of food prices. It chose a basket of representative types of food, and shopped in all those countries. This was the result: the least number of dollars was needed to buy this sample basket in the U.K. Canada was second, Australia third, the United States fourth, and so on. Prices were converted into U.S. dollars. It was a very significant result, in my view.
Take the over-all cost of living, again measured in U.S. dollars. Taking the U.S. dollar as 100 cents, the cost of buying the same amount of all goods was $1.02 in Canada, $1.04 in
[Mr. McRae.)
The Budget-Mr. McRae
the United Kingdom, and so on. We were second, the United States being First.
The next point has to do with inflation, that is, loss in purchasing power. It is measured on the basis of the same unit. This time it was the Canadian dollar, and of all those countries we come fourth in this period from 1970 to 1977. Our dollar is worth 60 cents, in West Germany the figure is 68 cents, in the United States, 64 cents and in Switzerland, 67 cents. Canada is fourth, with 60 cents. That is the way the purchasing power of the dollar is shrinking.
Take an index where we do not fare very well, that is, the balance of payments. In this group we come tenth out of 15. West Germany is first, followed by Japan. United States is eighth, very close to us. We do have a balance of payments problem. On the other hand, on the commodity trade side, the balance between exports and imports, Canada is third. We come out with $4.60 per capita, West Germany with $12.54, Australia with $7.31 and Canada was third.
In terms of housing starts, using 1970 and a base of 100, Canada is second with 126, Belgium is First with 152 and the United States third with 116.
Now take a very large item, the gross national product. Taking these 15 major countries, Japan is first with an average rise in the GNP per year of 7.36 per cent; France is second with 4.75 per cent; and Canada is third with 4.55 per cent. In the last year, (1977-78) Canada would be second with only Japan ahead of us.
In another area, hon. members on the other side are constantly going after the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner). He is defending himself ably, though. There is a reason: our industrial production has shown a larger increase than any of those countries. The country that is First, Norway, does not appear high up on any of the other lists. The second country is Canada, and the third is the United States. The increase for Canada is 32 per cent; Norway, 38 per cent; and the United States, 27 per cent.
United labour costs have declined for the period 1970 to 1977 in Canada by 5.6 per cent, and in the United States by 18.5 per cent. Canada is second, and the other 13 countries have done worse than we have, because their unit labour costs have risen faster than ours. Another point is the rise in real disposable income, the amount of income left after taxes. Here Canada is first. The graph is a little obscure, but it deals with a 2 per cent increase over this period. Japan was second.
If we put all these things together and if we give 15 points for each index to the country which has the most and then range down the list with one point going to the country with the least, when we total the points, we find that Canada gets 144 and comes first. This is not an accurate way of doing it, but it is the only way I know that can be done. The United States is second with 125 points. I am sure that if we were to do this, including the unemployment figure as one of the indices, Canada would still be well ahead of the other countries. During the period from the Arab boycott in 1974, to the

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. McRae
end of 1977, Canada would still be first. This is all plotted, but I do not have time to go through it.
Once again, the total points for each country are Canada, 144; the United States, 125; West Germany, 121; the Netherlands, fourth; Australia, fifth; Norway, sixth; Belgium, seventh; France, eighth; Finland, ninth; Japan, tenth; Italy, eleventh; Swizerland, twelfth; Denmark, thirteenth; United Kingdom, fourteenth; and Sweden, fifteenth.
There is something wrong when the bulk of the Canadian public believes that we are in such a terrible state, because if these OECD figures are true, then the rest of the world must be in unbelievable shape. This is the kind of misunderstanding that is fostered by the opposition. To some extent it is understandable because their purpose here is to oppose, but it is also taken up by the press. The press should be more aware in looking at this situation. But we on this side are also at fault because we have not explained the situation. We have not explained the relative position of Canada with the rest of the world in a careful way.
I am pleased to have this opportunity to put these facts before the House, and I hope that at least some Canadians will begin to see that our relative position has been very good and that we have fared rather well relative to other industrial countries. Canada is still the best country in which to live, and our economy has moved better than any other economy among these countries.
Very briefly, I would like to deal with some of the points in the budget. Many good economists today are saying that we are probably doing the best we can. Considering the general direction of the economy, the budget steps are probably as good as one can expect. I know that the other side will give me an argument, and legitimately so, about job creation. However, I do not think that there is any human way, short of doubling the deficit, that we can create a more substantial number of jobs than this government has created in the past seven or eight years. Canada is still ahead of everybody else, and we still have the problem of massive growth in the labour force-a problem that is unique to Canada-amounting to 500 per cent greater than any other country in the summit group. I do not have the figures for all 15 countries, but I do for the top seven, and we have a 500 per cent tougher job than the others.
The figure put out by the Economic Council of Canada that Canada's growth rate of 5 per cent-which is what everybody on the other side says we should have, even though the rest of the world will not achieve more than a 3 per cent or 3.5 per cent growth rate next year, except for Canada-will bring the unemployment rate down to 8 per cent. If the growth rate were to rise to 6 per cent, it would only reduce unemployment to 7.6 per cent.
There are answers, and redistribution of work is one of them. However, I do not think that we will solve the problem by dropping another $2 billion into the demand side, which is one of the alternatives proposed by Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. This is the same $2 billion we talked about back in the 1960s when we had a gross national product of $45 billion. Now we have a G.N.P. of $120 billion, and we are still using the
same $2 billion, which amounts to less than 1 per cent in its effect on unemployment today, and was about 4 per cent in the 1960s. I think that this kind of stimulus would only have a marginal effect.
The minister has rightly assumed that there will not likely be more than a 4 per cent to a 4.5 per cent growth in the economy next year. We are not likely to achieve a much higher rate of inflation next year than 6.5 per cent, perhaps 6 per cent toward the end of the year. The assumption is that we have done relatively well in all areas except in food, in spite of the condemnation of controls, and the food index should show an improvement.
The opposition has ignored some of the things in the budget. At one time we had a budget which would indicate a certain tax cut or increased exemptions. This is now automatic, and each year there are several billions of dollars going to the demand side. This year the exemption will be 9 per cent. If one looks at the revenue curve and the expenditure curve, one sees that they have paralleled each other over many years until 1974 when the government brought in this indexing system. Since that time the revenue curve has almost levelled off, and the expenditure curve has continued to rise. This is a problem with which the government must wrestle.
One thing in the budget which is rather important to me, and, I am sure, to all the members from northern Ontario, the Atlantic provinces and Gaspe, is the increase in the investment tax credit. This is a fundamental change which occurred last year. Also it is being brought into the Unemployment Insurance Act. Instead of devolving power to the provinces, as the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) would do if his party were in power, we decentralized some of the power. Not only do we decentralize people, we decentralize policy.
We have told the people of northern Ontario that they will receive an investment tax credit of up to 10 per cent, and up to 20 per cent in the Atlantic provinces. It is a change in the operation of government. Also, it applies to the regionalization of the Unemployment Insurance Act. These are answers to some of the problems articulated by hon. members on the other side. We are not turning the government of the country over to the provinces. We are attempting to make it work better as a national government.
I should like to refer to another aspect which affects northern Ontario. Because of the present value of our dollar at 85 or 86 cents, the woods industry, pulp and paper, logging, timber, and so on, is in very good shape at present. Most of the communities in northern Ontario dependent upon the lumber industry are doing well. In fact, Thunder Bay has the lowest unemployment rate of any Canadian city. That has been the case for over a year. This fact is attributed directly to the state of the dollar and the fact that this industry is involved in the export business.
Communities involved in the mining industry have not had the same success. I am pleased that the budget contained a write-off increase from 30 per cent to 100 per cent for mining

November 21, 1978

development. Also there were increased write-offs for town sites, social purposes and so on. Because of depressed prices of various minerals on world markets, the mining industry is depressed. These extra write-offs certainly will help communities in northern Ontario.
In conclusion, given the state of the Canadian economy, the relative good performance of our economy, the best of all industrial nations in the world, and the difficulties faced by all 15 industrial countries, the budget is extremely appropriate to the nature of the country and the nature of our times.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to take part in this budget debate because it gives me an opportunity to commend the minister for some measures he has taken, to offer constructive criticism, and to express my disappointment at some measures which have not been included.
I like the $500 employee expense deduction which will confer upon working Canadians some of the tax benefits already enjoyed by professional and business people. The decrease in the manufacturers' sales tax will help to stimulate the economy to the extent it is passed on to consumers. The increased tax incentives for research and development and the increase in the investment tax credit will be beneficial to Canadian business, particularly small business. The improvement in resource taxes is long overdue.
However, the over-all impact of the budget falls far short of Canada's needs. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) seems to be telling us in many ways to expect another year of economic stagnation, as well as a further deterioration in the federal government's fiscal position. Of the $1.3 billion loss to the federal treasury, it would seem that only $300 million will be returned in increased tax revenues. Clearly the economy needs greater stimulus.
I am disappointed the federal government did not choose to adopt our proposal for deductibility of mortgage interest and property taxes from personal income taxes. This proposal in itself would have given the Canadian economy a bigger boost than the entire budget.
There are over 7 million households in Canada and 4.6 million home owners. This reflects the strong desire of Canadians to own their own homes. But in 1975, the last year for which income figures are available, only 9 per cent of Canadians could afford to buy the average new house which was then priced at $42,800. It is socially desirable that Canadians who wish to own their own homes have a reasonable opportunity to do so. These measures would make the Canadian income tax system at least as attractive as that in the United States.
A key difference between the two systems is that the Americans are able to deduct both mortgage interest and property taxes from their annual income. This results in a major reduction in the financing of home ownership for Americans. While the American system allows for mortgage interest and property tax deductibility in all residences, the
The Budget-Mr. Howie
plan which we propose would allow deductibility on principal residences only. This program would provide a major stimulus to the economy by returning significant amounts of after tax dollars to Canadian consumers on a permanent basis.
The depressed rate of consumer spending is a critical weakness in the Canadian economy at present. In fact, a recovery in consumer spending, a stimulus to the building industry, and an increased accumulation of private pools of capital are central to a revitalized economic growth. Clearly these measures would allow more Canadians to purchase their own homes by returning significant amounts of money to them. The effect of increased home purchases will be a major stimulus both to the Canadian home furnishings and construction industries which are almost wholly domestic.
On November 14 of last year, I placed a question on the order paper concerning the revenue loss of tax deductions of interest payable on mortgages on residences. The answer from the Department of Finance indicated that the department had analysed this proposal. The revenue loss would depend upon the structure of the measure and what sort of limits were applied. It could be as high as $1.5 billion per year. On the question of permitting income tax deductions of municipal property taxes, again the Department of Finance indicated that it had analysed the proposal, that the revenue loss would depend upon the structure of the measure and what sort of limitations were applied. It could be well over $500 billion. Thus, we have an indication of the cost of these measures from the government. One measure to reduce the cost is to phase the program over a four-year period. Another restriction measure is to place a limit of $5,000 per year on the allowable interest deduction and a ceiling of $1,000 a year in respect of property taxes.
The benefit to an average Canadian can be measured by taking as an example a family of four with one working spouse, two children, a home with a $30,000 mortgage and annual property taxes of $500. This is not an unusual Canadian situation. It is a good example. This family would gain $197 in reduced taxes in the first year of the program, and $756 when the program is fully in place. This would be a real stimulus to consumer purchasing. It would put more Canadians to work in the building trades and sell more Canadian materials. It would create more Canadian taxpayers. It would help our economy to move forward again. It would help renew consumer and investor confidence.
This program of mortgage interest and property tax deductions, like the programs the minister proposed, can be financed by increases in the gross domestic product and hence our revenues, without increasing taxes, or by identifying programs of a lower priority where expenditures can be eliminated. The government has announced a restraint program. We will be watching to see if it continues restraint in a meaningful manner. The projected deficit of 34 per cent in federal revenues is a record for Canada and one of the highest in the western world. It is a record which is not really wanted. But like the ghost of Christmas past, it has come back to haunt the current Minister of Finance and to restrict severely the area in

November 21, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Howie
which he can manoeuvre in his very serious battle against both inflation and high employment.
I would like to leave some thoughts with the minister in his search for restraint. I suggest that he take another look at the $1.4 billion we pay out to consultants, in an attempt to determine if some of these services could be supplied by other departments of government. Information advertising expenditures have increased remarkably over the years to somewhere around $ 180 million.
I know that Crown corporations have a necessary role to play in the structure of government, but I do believe that periodically they should justify their continued existence as government agencies. That is not to suggest that they have to go out of business, but once their role exceeds the necessary function of the government, it seems to me the government would be quite justified in giving the private sector of our economy an opportunity to assume the risk of owning and operating the business by purchasing it from the government. We have long debated the merits of Petro-Can, Eldorado Nuclear, Canadair and Northern Transportation Limited. Without repeating the arguments pro and con, I would be inclined to add to the list the Canadian Commercial Corporation.
One feature of the budget I find highly commendable is the special provisions to encourage research and development by small Canadian businesses. Such businesses qualify for the low rate of corporation tax and will get an investment tax credit of 25 per cent of their research and development expenditures, irrespective of their location in Canada. This measure, coupled with the proposal to double the basic rate of investment tax credit for research and development from 5 per cent to 10 per cent, which is set at 20 per cent in the Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe, is a good measure.
I thought the 25 per cent tax credit for research and development was an excellent idea, and I said so in this House on June 21 last when I spoke in respect of Bill C-56. I would like to say so again today. My colleague, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), was one of several members who did considerable work on research and development issues which were debated in the last budget debate and under Clause 6 of Bill C-56. With background help, various substantive amendments were made which would have improved all industrial aspects of research and development in Canada, and would have put in place very real incentives which would have worked to smooth out this area of need in the Canadian economy. These amendments were passed on to the government during committee of the whole debate on that bill, and they were suggested as being superior to the measures which the government had proposed at that time.
One other measure which was proposed by my colleagues and myself at that time, and which I would like to recommend for the consideration of the minister now, is that in arriving at the definition of a small business in order to stimulate research and development, we consider the amount of research and
development carried out by a small business. I suggest that for purposes of this tax credit, any business in Canada which does less than $1 million worth in research and development in a fiscal year should be considered a small business.
The present federal government tax incentive program is inadequate in the following respects: The incentive is based on incremental research and development expenditures only; the consolidation of capital with current expenditures penalizes firms making substantial capital outlay for R and D purposes; the incentive discriminates severely against the smaller firms whose net cost of R and D could be 70 per cent higher than for larger firms, and the incentive is not available to firms not having a taxable income, for example in the start-up phase of new technology-based firms.
When the minister has an opportunity to refer back to the debate I have mentioned, as reported at pages 6626 to 6632 of Hansard, he will find some very helpful suggestions along these lines made by colleagues.
I would like to suggest that any review of industrial support policies should involve the full participation of industry. New incentive programs should minimize elaborate administration. For example, where applicable, self-administered tax credits are preferable to grants which require lengthy and complex applications and detailed monitoring. The contracting out of government R and D projects, which have been a step in the right direction, should be intensified.
Federal procurement policy should aim to stimulate promising Canadian companies. The procurement policies of local and provincial governments, as well as publicly supported institutions, should be similarly co-ordinated. The federal government should take the lead by making this a condition of various incentives and cost-sharing programs. International trade and technological agreements should make special provisions to strengthen Canada's industrial capacity. Opportunities for co-operative activities should be sought out and supported. Fragmentation and polarization of the activities of various groups, whether in industry, government or universities, must be overcome. Eventually, incentive programs and other related activities that are designed to affect industry should be developed in the context of a comprehensive industrial strategy which would support the emergence of strong, stable Canadian companies and rationalize Canadian industrial capacities to meet industrial competition. This latter thought has been expressed and underscored by Dr. Kates and the Science Council.
It is imperative that we create a more attractive climate for technological innovation in Canada, if the research and development performed by a parent company in respect of the output of Canadian subsidiaries is to be expanded in Canada.
Our tax incentives must be strong enough to make it attractive and profitable to perform the research and development in Canada, and as a precondition to receiving any such incentive, R and D must in fact be done in Canada.
The bottom line is that it is not enough to have the best tax incentive system in the western world. Our ministers, deputy


ministers, assistant deputy ministers and department heads have to get on their bicycles and travel to the board rooms of the parent companies of Canadian subsidiaries and sell our program. We have to give the private sector the confidence that our government understands that research is a long-term proposition, and convince them that the incentives will remain in position and be constant for at least ten years.
In the past 15 years we have witnessed a number of major unrelated programs involving tax incentives put forward and then cancelled by the present government. It is small wonder that the private sector takes no confidence in this performance and is not prepared to commit its funds to a program of long-term scientific research and innovation.
Prior to 1962, Canadian firms could deduct 100 per cent of their current capital expenditures for tax purposes. In 1962, an amendment to the Income Tax Act added a new section, section 72(a), which provided an additional tax deduction of 50 per cent of the increase in research and development expenditures for capital and current costs over the 1961 level. This special allowance was replaced about five years later by the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act, and late in 1975 this program too came to a grinding halt, but it was not immediately replaced. The make or buy policy was then in force and the PAIT program was also in place, but neither of these could be classified as a tax incentive.
Last year the tax investment credit was announced. Earlier this year the government moved the clock back to 1962 by returning to the special tax deduction allowance feature for income tax purposes. Now the government has had the wisdom to take a step in the right direction with the current proposal of a 25 per cent tax credit.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-RCMP INVESTIGATION OF BOEING CONTRACT-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-RCMP INVESTIGATION OF BOEING CONTRACT-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight because of an unsatisfactory answer I received yesterday to a question I put to the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais). I asked the Solicitor General, as recorded at page 1263 of Hansard, what progress had been made with the investigation into kickbacks that were paid in Canada by the Boeing Air-
Adjournment Debate
craft Company concerning deals whereby Canada bought aircraft from Boeing.
There were five companies in Canada that did buy aircraft from Boeing, and this might have happened to any one of them. These included the Department of Supply and Services of the Canadian government, Air Canada, Eastern Provincial Airways, Nordair and Transair.
Somewhere in Canada there is a crook who has gypped Canada. Some 20 months after the first clear indication, and four months after absolute declaration that there is a crook in our midst, nothing seems to be happening. Progress is far too slow. India has out-distanced us in this. I would like tonight to point out why we should have moved considerably faster.
First of all I would like to read from a complaint by the Securities Exchange Commission of the United States which commenced a suit against the Boeing aircraft company requiring it to conduct its business so it was no longer fraudulent. On examination of the documents provided by Boeing we find the following stated:
In some instances, Boeing used dual consulting contracts with identical terms except for the compensation payable to the consultant. One contract provided for nominal compensation to the consultant while the second contract specified payments of additional compensation to the consultant-
I suggest there is no way that the Securities and Exchange Commission could look at these dual contracts without realizing that they were made out to the same person. There is no way they could make that statement unless the same person's name appeared on both contracts. If it did, the Securities and Exchange Commission of the United States must know the person to whom those dual contracts were made out.
Further on in the same complaint the Securities and Exchange Commission had this to say:
Certain of these disbursements were improperly described as commissions on the books and records of Boeing. All of such payments were made to nominee and conduit accounts in Switzerland.
Once again, if they knew to what consultant they were made out, they must have had the consultant's name.
If I have established that the Securities and Exchange Commission knew the name of the consultant who took double payments, then why should Canada not have made faster progress than it has? I refer to a news release dated March 15, 1977 when Canada signed an agreement with the United States. In the news release which accompanied the agreement issued by the then Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Basford) this passage appears:
The agreement provides that following requests for assistance, the United States Department of Justice and the Department of Justice of Canada will assist each other in making available relevant information and material pertaining to the sales activities in Canada of The Boeing Company-
In the first paragraph of the agreement itself appears the words "with respect to alleged illicit acts pertaining to the sales activities in Canada of The Boeing Company." This quite clearly establishes that illegal acts had been taking place as

November 21, 1978
Adjournment Debate
early as 20 months ago. Paragraph 2 of the agreement goes on to state:
-the parties shall use their best efforts to make available to each other relevant and material information, such as statements, depositions, documents, business records, correspondence or other materials-
I submit that should include the name of the culprit.
I should like to point out that during this time Canada has asked the United States department of justice about this and has received co-operation, at least according to the Minister of Justice who answered me on this matter about a month ago. I therefore cannot understand the delay in laying charges against the culprits.
I particularly want to point out that it is quite clear from the evidence before us that these complaints were filed by the SEC before the United States district court for the District of Columbia. The district court of the District of Columbia records are available to the United States department of justice. Since they are made available to the department of justice of the United States, according to our agreement they should be delivered to us if we ask for them. If we have not asked for them, we should do so immediately. If we have asked for them, then the name should be in the hands of our government. I want to know from the minister why nothing has been done and why we cannot seem to make any progress whatever.
A month ago the Solicitor General's parliamentary secretary said that we would have the information soon. Yesterday, he was not as promising. He gave no date and said that he could not guarantee when the final report of the RCMP would be in his hands. I should like those two questions answered tonight, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-INQUIRY AS TO FINANCIAL MEASURES TAKEN TO REDUCE NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED
LABOUR CONDITIONS-INQUIRY AS TO FINANCIAL MEASURES TAKEN TO REDUCE NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 7 I asked the Minister of Finance a question

concerning the measures he intended to submit to the House in order to reduce the number of unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, this question as reported on page 866 of Hansard was the following:
According to a recent article Canada is in the leading position on the world wide level as far as unemployment is concerned. This is not in accordance with the statements made by the Minister of Finance. The article says that Canada has a record 8.5 per cent of unemployed.
I asked the minister what he intended to propose in his budget to try to further develop the use of our manpower in order to increase our gross national product to become as prosperous as the other industrial countries in the western world. The minister said that he required a complete budget to give a thorough answer to my serious question and that he regretted that our unemployment level was so high. He added that in that last 12 months we had created 362,000 new jobs in Canada and that our performance as far as job creation was concerned was not equalled by any country in the world.
Mr. Speaker, it is not a pleasure for me to tackle this question nor is it my intention to embarrass the government. We hear so many complaints that there is no point in raising questions likely to put the government in trouble. What we want in this parliament is that the government face up to its responsibilities and solve the situation in a clever and efficient way.
Mr. Speaker, I would like very briefly to prove the seriousness of my question, with some figures on the level of unemployment in eastern Quebec. Especially in my own area of Bellechasse. Unemployment in Bellechasse is not due to its having a Social Credit MP, because there is just as much in any other constituency in the province of Quebec and the rest of Canada. It is because we have the same system as everywhere else.
The head of Montmagny's Manpower Centre, Mr. Claude Boileau, whose photograph appeared in the local newspaper Peuple Courrier, was quoted as saying in July that the level of unemployment is nearly a quarter of the work force. Later, figures were published concerning communities under the jurisdiction of the Montmagny Manpower Centre. The total population is 23,401, the labour force is 7,090 and the number of unemployed 1,663. The number of unemployed female is 492, on a total 2,155. This is becoming serious when there is a 7,090 work force. Another table shows there are 1,346 men receiving unemployment benefits and 317 people receiving other help, for a total 1,663 people out of 7,090 capable of working. This means there are a number of other people that are without revenue or live off welfare.
The situation is therefore, disquieting, and we must absolutely see to it that the number of people looking for work be reduced. Some will say, and perhaps they are right, that there may be some people who have not worked for such a long time
November 21, 1978

that they have lost the desire to work and no longer understand that work is normal and that it is a tool which must be used to earn a living and to transform in detail what God has given us to meet the needs of men. God could have created everything ready for consumption, but He wanted men to join Him in His work of creation. This is why He has given us this tool of work. The public authorities, the governments, must find the means to close the gap when the private sector cannot absorb all the manpower available. This is the role of the government, to intervene through public works to absorb this manpower, to maintain this desire to work and to give those who want to work the possibility of supporting themselves honourably.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government has established various programs, including Canada Works, within its field of responsibility. Some projects submitted under this program may not be very good and some may be quite bad. However, I believe that the quality of projects has improved a lot in the last few years, and I want to pay tribute to the people of my constituency who go to the trouble of submitting useful projects. However, when these projects are implemented, they should not cause us problems such as that which occurred last week with a project in my constituency when the mayor offered his services free of charge to help the residents of the municipality. He was provided with the funds required to implement a project which would have enabled him to build sidewalks and repair his municipal workshop. And three days after the work started an inspector from the Quebec Construction Office came and ordered him to stop the works and told him he would be penalized and fined unless he had a good member of parliament to defend him. So the mayor, a very intelligent man, told him: It is incredible, you set the fire and then you say: If you have a good member, he will put it out.
Mr. Speaker, that kind of situation is not acceptable in a Christian and civilized society. I think that an agreement should be possible between federal and provincial authorities so that we can really work and ensure public services and employment opportunities for the people.
Mr. Speaker, I brought that matter to the attention of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) who committed himself to communicate with the Quebec labour minister. So I hope that consultations have begun and that they will have positive results so that such situations will not reoccur.
Mr. Speaker, here is the most efficient measure that the government can take to lighten the unemployment burden: public works. As recently as last week, I received representations from municipalities asking that retaining walls be built along the St. Lawrence River because every year the water eats away part of the riverside properties.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-INQUIRY AS TO FINANCIAL MEASURES TAKEN TO REDUCE NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat embarrassed in answering my friend, my colleague from Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), as I have before me an answer written in the other official language, so I must answer in that language and I hope he will excuse me for that.

As the hon. member has indicated, unemployment in Canada has recently been at a level of 8.5 per cent of the labour force. However, it should be noted that in October the unemployment rate dropped to a seasonally adjusted rate of 8.2 per cent, the lowest rate registered in over a year.
Because our labour force has been growing much more rapidly than in other industrialized countries-since 1970 about 3'/2 per cent a year, compared to 2 per cent for the U.S., under 1 per cent for the U.K., France and Japan, and a decline for Germany-unemployment has reached very high levels, despite the rapid increase in the number of Canadians who are working. Employment increased by more than 3.6 per cent in the last year, and 362,000 more Canadians are working today than one year ago.
One of the main reasons for the fast growth of the labour force is the rapidly growing participation of Canadian women in the labour force.
Another important reason for the growth of the labour force has been a surge of young people coming into the labour market. This surge is not expected to last. The population in the 15 to 19-year-old age group is expected to decline after 1979. However, the immediate challenge has been to create enough jobs for all our young people and to alleviate other structural unemployment problems.
In the field of manpower-training and job creation, the government has recently announced an employment strategy for 1979-80 which continues the key objective of increasing the employment and employability of all Canadians, while shifting the emphasis to helping industry train and employ Canadians, and particularly young job seekers.
A main feature of the 1979-80 employment strategy is the development of a strategy to increase youth employment, particularly in the private sector, at a cost of $225 million. The summer youth employment program will be expanded, which includes programs such as Young Canada Works, Summer Job Corps, and so on. Expenditures will be increased on year round youth employment and employability programs, Youth Job Corps-a new program-job experience training, and so on, from $14.5 million this fiscal year to nearly $110 million in 1979-80. It is expected that the JET program alone will provide private sector employment and experience to over 63,000 youth in 1979-80.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-REQUEST HOUSE BE INFORMED OF REASONS FOR RAISING INTEREST RATES
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-REQUEST HOUSE BE INFORMED OF REASONS FOR RAISING INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my questions arise out of questions I asked in the House on November 6 concerning the rise in the interest rate announced the day previous to my questions. In asking my questions, I brought to the minister's attention the fact that the rise in the interest rate represented something far more serious than the government appreciated at that time.
In considering the financial measures brought in by this government, we have to take all things in context. For example, we have to take the budget in context, not only of the cutbacks announced on August 1 by the government, but also in the context of the rise in the rate of interest which has taken place since January of this year.
This rise brings us to the unprecedented point where our interest rate is at 10% per cent. Our concern is that the impact of this increase and the effect it will have right through the economy has not been sufficiently appreciated by the government in bringing down its budget.
In his evidence on November 6, the main rationale expressed by Governor Bouey was that he was preoccupied with the concern that unless we did something about our interest rates to keep them at a higher percentage than the American rate, Canada's dollar would decline and we would be in a very dangerous position. He described it as depreciating our way into inflation. The governor referred to the British disease. Members of the official opposition referred to the danger of Canada catching the British disease. That disease manifests itself if a currency depreciates too quickly and the cost of imports go way up. That will have an effect on inflation right through the economy.
In attempting to avoid catching the British disease, we are subject to another disease which can be called the Canadian disease. The Canadian disease in respect of the economy and high interest rates is our dependence on the U.S. If the Americans take a decision with regard to American interest rates, that decision is based on a set of decisions which apply in the United States. However, the same concern as would lead to a decision being taken in the United States with respect to its economy, may have nothing to do with the decision taken with respect to our economy. So in effect we are taking a decision over which we have no genuine control as a result of a decision made in the United States. I do not say this out of any knee-jerk anti-Americanism or anything of that kind. That is not the case on my part. My concern is that in responding to what basically it sees as external requirements, the need to guarantee that the Canadian dollar does not fall below 85 cents, the government is tying itself to a high rate of interest for a considerable time-I suggest it has no idea when interest rates will go down in the United States.
Answering my question, the minister said he would take into account the problems of the interest rate when he brought down his budget. I see no evidence whatever that the budget
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
will be able to provide an antidote to these serious inflationary measures affecting the economy. Therefore, without being a prophet of gloom or doom, the question I direct to the parliamentary secretary is this: if the government intends to carry out a policy of high interest rates, can he not tell us what policies it intends to carry out at the same time to make sure we do not sacrifice our internal strength, our industrial strength and our economic health to the need to protect our foreign exchange markets?
This is a dilemma. It is one which the government has not faced straight on. It seems to me we are sacrificing much of our industrial health to maintain the standard of the dollar and in following this policy, in attempting to avoid the British disease, we are in danger of getting the Canadian disease. Many military men are accused of fighting wars that are already over, instead of addressing themselves to the circumstances of today. In the same way, economists would be well advised to fight the current war instead of seeking to apply solutions which are now outmoded. I fear there will be serious deflation as a result of the government's determination, I would say blind determination, to keep our interest rates one point ahead of rates in America.

speakeroldname: Mr. Alan Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-REQUEST HOUSE BE INFORMED OF REASONS FOR RAISING INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in beginning my response I should repeat the comment made by the minister at the time he replied to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae). He stated clearly that it is the Governor of the Bank of Canada who establishes the interest rate. It is not the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who makes that decision.
The decision to raise interest rates required a balancing of judgments of the consequences of raising them against the consequences of not raising them.
The bank and the government would have preferred not to have been faced with the need to make this difficult decision, but the move by the U.S. authorities forced us to consider the consequences for Canada of higher interest rates in the U.S.
If the higher interest rates in the U.S. were likely to lead to an outflow of capital from Canada, a resumption of the decline in the value of our currency and an increase in the cost of imports and domestic production, this would be damaging to domestic stability and our capacity to employ Canadians. These consequences would develop quickly but linger to plague our economic performance for some time. In arriving at a decision they are to be compared with the restraining effects of higher interest rates. It is not possible to predict when circumstances may change, but when they do, we can contemplate lower interest rates again.
Higher interest rates are certainly an element of increased cost to business. The risk was that without an increase in interest rates we might get other costs rising and built more permanently into the cost structure of Canadian industry.
The policy of the government continues to be to seek to establish the conditions for further declines in our prices and
November 21, 1978

costs so as to consolidate our improved competitive position in order that we may, with renewed confidence, increase our share of world markets and our ability to satisfy our own needs. That is the surest way to increase the employment of our growing labour force. It is our judgment that the action taken on Sunday night-to which the hon. member has referred-in the face of the U.S. move, is much more con-
Adjournment Debate
sistent with this objective than a policy of no action would have been.
